docs.title: Numerical Problem 1: Wasted Slots Fraction in Slotted Broadcast Subnet
Problem Statement
docs.text: A broadcast channel with \(n\) contending hosts operates in discrete slots. Each host attempts to transmit with probability \(p\) during each slot. Derive the exact fraction of slots wasted due to collisions.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Define the complete set of mutually exclusive outcomes for any slot:
  2. Event 1 (Success by specific station \(i\)): Station \(i\) transmits (\(p\)), remaining \((n-1)\) stations remain silent (\((1-p)^{n-1}\)).
\[ P(\text{Host } i \text{ succeeds}) = p(1-p)^{n-1} \]
  • Total Success Probability (\(P_{\text{success}}\)): Any one of the \(n\) stations succeeds:
\[ P_{\text{success}} = n p (1 - p)^{n-1} \]
  • Idle Channel Probability (\(P_{\text{idle}}\)): No station transmits:
\[ P_{\text{idle}} = (1 - p)^n \]
  • Collision Probability (\(P_{\text{collision}}\)): Two or more stations transmit.
  • Since total probability sums to 1:
\[ P_{\text{collision}} = 1 - P_{\text{success}} - P_{\text{idle}} = 1 - n p(1 - p)^{n-1} - (1 - p)^n \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Fraction of Wasted Slots: \(1 - n p(1 - p)^{n-1} - (1 - p)^n\)

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Pages 2–3]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 2: Delay of Pure ALOHA vs Slotted ALOHA at Low Load
Problem Statement
docs.text: Consider the delay of Pure ALOHA versus Slotted ALOHA at very low traffic load (\(G \approx 0\)). Which protocol exhibits lower transmission delay, and why?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. In Pure ALOHA, a station transmits immediately the instant a frame is generated, with zero alignment delay. At low load (\(G \to 0\)), collisions are negligible, so average delay is simply the frame transmission time:
\[ T_{\text{Pure}} = T_f \]
  1. In Slotted ALOHA, a station generating a frame at a random time must wait for the start of the next slot. On average, this waiting time is half a slot ($ \frac{1}{2} T_f$). The total delay is:
\[ T_{\text{Slotted}} = T_f + 0.5 T_f = 1.5 T_f \]
  1. Therefore, at light load, Pure ALOHA has less delay because it does not incur the average half-slot synchronization waiting time.

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Lower Delay at Low Load: Pure ALOHA (\(T = T_f\) vs \(1.5 T_f\) for Slotted ALOHA).

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 4; cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 3, Q3]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3: ALOHA Success Probabilities for 50 Requests/sec
Problem Statement
docs.text: A large population of ALOHA users generates \(50\text{ requests/sec}\) (including originals and retransmissions) on a slotted channel with slot duration \(T_f = 40\text{ ms} = 0.040\text{ s}\). 1. What is the probability of success on the first attempt? 2. What is the probability of exactly \(k\) collisions followed by a success? 3. What is the expected number of transmission attempts per frame?

docs.title: Given Values
docs.text:
• Arrival rate: \(\lambda = 50\text{ frames/sec}\)
  • Slot duration: \(T_f = 0.040\text{ sec}\)
  • Offered load per slot: \(G = \lambda \times T_f = 50 \times 0.040 = 2.0\)

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. In Slotted ALOHA, probability of zero other transmissions in a slot is:
\[ P_{\text{success}} = e^{-G} = e^{-2} = \f\frac{1}{e^2} \approx 0.135335 \approx 13.53\% \]
  1. Let \(P = e^{-2}\) be the probability of success in any attempt. The probability of failure (collision) is \(q = 1 - P = 1 - e^{-2} \approx 0.864665\). The probability of experiencing exactly \(k\) collisions and then succeeding on attempt \((k+1)\) follows a geometric distribution:
\[ P(k \text{ collisions then success}) = (1 - e^{-2})^k e^{-2} = q^k P \]
  1. The expected number of transmission attempts \(E[N]\) for a geometric random variable is:
\[ E[N] = \f\frac{1}{P} = \f\frac{1}{e^{-2}} = e^2 \approx 7.389\text{ attempts} \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• (a) First Attempt Success: \(e^{-2} \approx 13.53\%\)
  • (b) Probability of \(k\) Collisions then Success: \(e^{-2} (1 - e^{-2})^k\)
  • (c) Expected Attempts: \(e^2 \approx 7.39\text{ attempts}\)

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Pages 5–7; cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 3, Q4]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 4: CSMA/CD Contention Slot Duration in Cable vs Fiber
Problem Statement
docs.text: Calculate the duration of a contention slot (\(2\tau\)) in CSMA/CD for: 1. A \(2\text{ km}\) twin-lead cable where signal propagation speed is \(82\%\) of the speed of light in vacuum (\(c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\)). 2. A \(40\text{ km}\) multimode optical fiber where signal propagation speed is \(65\%\) of the speed of light in vacuum.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. For Twin-Lead Cable (\(D = 2000\text{ m}\)):
  2. Velocity: \(v = 0.82 \times 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} = 2.46 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
  3. One-way delay: \(\tau = \f\frac{2000\text{ m}}{2.46 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = 8.13 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s} = 8.13\,\mu\text{s}\).
  4. Contention slot: \(2\tau = 2 \times 8.13\,\mu\text{s} = 16.26\,\mu\text{s} \approx 16.3\,\mu\text{s}\).
  5. For Multimode Fiber (\(D = 40,000\text{ m}\)):
  6. Velocity: \(v = 0.65 \times 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} = 1.95 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
  7. One-way delay: \(\tau = \f\frac{40,000\text{ m}}{1.95 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = 2.051 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s} = 205.13\,\mu\text{s}\).
  8. Contention slot: \(2\tau = 2 \times 205.13\,\mu\text{s} = 410.26\,\mu\text{s} \approx 410\,\mu\text{s}\).

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• (a) 2-km Cable Contention Slot: \(16.26\,\mu\text{s}\)
  • (b) 40-km Fiber Contention Slot: \(410.26\,\mu\text{s}\)

[Source: cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 4, Q1]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 5: Worst-Case Delay in Bit-Map Protocol
Problem Statement
docs.text: How long does a station \(s\) have to wait in the worst case before it can start transmitting its frame over a LAN that uses the basic bit-map protocol with \(N\) stations and data frame size of \(d\) bits?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Suppose Station \(s\) generates a frame immediately after its own slot (\(s\)) in the reservation bitmap has passed.
  2. Station \(s\) must wait for the remaining \((N - s - 1)\) reservation bits of the current contention period.
  3. Then, in the worst case, all \(N\) stations have reserved frames in this cycle, requiring \(N \times d\) bit times.
  4. Then, the next contention period begins, requiring \(s\) reservation bit times before station \(s\) can assert its 1 bit.
  5. Then, all lower-numbered stations (\(0\) to \(s-1\)) transmit their data frames (\(s \times d\) bits).
  6. Total worst-case waiting time:
\[ T_{\text{wait, worst}} = N + N \cdot d = N(d + 1)\text{ bit times} \]

(Or in terms of bitmap slots before reservation: \(N\) contention bits).

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Worst-case Waiting Time: \(N(d + 1)\text{ bit times}\) (or \(N\) reservation slots).

[Source: cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 4, Q2; CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 8]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 6: IP Packet Padding in Ethernet Frames
Problem Statement
docs.text: An IP packet to be transmitted by Ethernet is 60 bytes long, including all its headers. If LLC (IEEE 802.2) is not in use, is padding needed in the Ethernet frame, and if so, how many bytes?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Standard Ethernet (Ethernet II) header overhead consists of:
  2. Destination MAC Address: 6 Bytes
  3. Source MAC Address: 6 Bytes
  4. EtherType Field: 2 Bytes
  5. FCS Checksum: 4 Bytes
  6. Total Header/Trailer Overhead = \(6 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 18\text{ Bytes}\).
  7. Total frame size without padding:
\[ \text{Total Frame Size} = 18\text{ Bytes (Overhead)} + 60\text{ Bytes (IP Packet)} = 78\text{ Bytes} \]
  1. The minimum required Ethernet frame size is 64 Bytes.
  2. Since \(78\text{ Bytes} > 64\text{ Bytes}\), the frame already exceeds the minimum frame size requirement.

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Padding Needed: No padding is needed (0 bytes padding). Total frame size is \(78\text{ Bytes}\).

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 9; cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 4, Q3]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 7: Fast Ethernet Cable Length Scaling
Problem Statement
docs.text: Ethernet frames must be at least 64 bytes long to ensure the transmitter can detect collisions. Fast Ethernet has the same 64-byte minimum frame size but transmits 10 times faster (\(100\text{ Mbps}\) vs \(10\text{ Mbps}\)). How is it possible to maintain the same minimum frame size without losing collision detection?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. The minimum frame length equation is:
\[ L_{\min} = 2 \cdot \left(\f\frac{D}{v}\r\right) \cdot B = \f\frac{2 D B}{v} \]
  1. For Fast Ethernet:
  2. Bandwidth \(B_{\text{Fast}} = 10 \times B_{\text{Classic}}\).
  3. Minimum frame size \(L_{\min}\) remains fixed at \(64\text{ Bytes} = 512\text{ bits}\).
  4. Velocity \(v\) remains unchanged.
  5. Equating formulas:
\[ L_{\min} = \f\frac{2 D_{\text{Fast}} (10 B)}{v} = \f\frac{2 D_{\text{Classic}} B}{v} \implies D_{\text{Fast}} = \f\frac{D_{\text{Classic}}}{10} \]
  1. Therefore, the maximum allowable network span (cable length) must be reduced by a factor of 10 (from \(2500\text{ m}\) down to \(250\text{ m}\) / \(100\text{ m}\) per segment).

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Method to Maintain 64B Size: Reduce maximum cable span by factor of 10 (\(D_{\text{Fast}} = \f\frac{1}{10} D_{\text{Classic}}\)).

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 10; cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 4, Q4]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 8: CSMA/CD Minimum Frame Length for 10 km Network
Problem Statement
docs.text: Assume CSMA/CD protocol. Find the minimum frame length for a \(1\text{ Mbps}\) network with a maximum span of \(10\text{ km}\) and no repeaters. Assume medium propagation delay is \(4.5\text{ ns/meter}\). Is CSMA/CD reasonable for this network?

docs.title: Given Values
docs.text:
• Bandwidth: \(B = 1\text{ Mbps} = 10^6\text{ bps}\)
  • Distance: \(D = 10\text{ km} = 10,000\text{ m}\)
  • Propagation delay per meter: \(4.5\text{ ns/m} = 4.5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ s/m}\)

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. One-way propagation delay:
\[ \tau = 10,000\text{ m} \times 4.5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ s/m} = 4.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ seconds} = 45\,\mu\text{s} \]
  1. Round-trip time:
\[ 2\tau = 2 \times 4.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s} = 9.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s} = 90\,\mu\text{s} \]
  1. Minimum frame length:
\[ L_{\min} = B \times 2\tau = (10^6\text{ bps}) \times (9.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s}) = 90\text{ bits} = 11.25\text{ Bytes} \]
  1. Since \(11.25\text{ Bytes}\) is very small and well below typical frame sizes (e.g. 64 bytes), CSMA/CD is extremely reasonable for this network.

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Minimum Frame Length: \(90\text{ bits}\) (\(11.25\text{ Bytes}\))
  • Feasibility: Highly reasonable protocol for this span and bitrate.

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 11]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 9: Adaptive Tree Walk Contention Slots Resolution
Problem Statement
docs.text: Sixteen stations (numbered 1 through 16) contend for a shared channel using the Adaptive Tree Walk protocol. If all stations whose addresses are prime numbers (Stations 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13) become ready at once, how many bit slots are needed to resolve contention?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text: Stations ready to send: \(\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13\}\). * Slot 1 (Node 1–16): Stations \(\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13\}\) contend \(\implies\) Collision. Split into Left \(\{1–8\}\) and Right \(\{9–16\}\). * Slot 2 (Node 1–8): Stations \(\{2, 3, 5, 7\}\) contend \(\implies\) Collision. Split into \(\{1–4\}\) and \(\{5–8\}\). * Slot 3 (Node 1–4): Stations \(\{2, 3\}\) contend \(\implies\) Collision. Split into \(\{1–2\}\) and \(\{3–4\}\). * Slot 4 (Node 1–2): Only Station \(\{2\}\) contends \(\implies\) Success (Station 2). * Slot 5 (Node 3–4): Only Station \(\{3\}\) contends \(\implies\) Success (Station 3). * Slot 6 (Node 5–8): Stations \(\{5, 7\}\) contend \(\implies\) Collision. Split into \(\{5–6\}\) and \(\{7–8\}\). * Slot 7 (Node 5–6): Only Station \(\{5\}\) contends \(\implies\) Success (Station 5). * Slot 8 (Node 7–8): Only Station \(\{7\}\) contends \(\implies\) Success (Station 7). * Slot 9 (Node 9–16): Stations \(\{11, 13\}\) contend \(\implies\) Collision. Split into \(\{9–12\}\) and \(\{13–16\}\). * Slot 10 (Node 9–12): Only Station \(\{11\}\) contends \(\implies\) Success (Station 11). * Slot 11 (Node 13–16): Only Station \(\{13\}\) contends \(\implies\) Success (Station 13).

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Total Slots Needed: 11 bit slots

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 12]

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Consider five wireless stations A, B, C, D, E with communication ranges: * A can communicate with B, C, D, E. * B can communicate with A, C, E. * C can communicate with A, B, D. * D can communicate with A, C, E. * E can communicate with A, B, D.

Determine concurrent communication possibilities: 1. When A is sending to B, what other communications are possible? 2. When B is sending to A, what other communications are possible? 3. When B is sending to C, what other communications are possible?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Case (a) A sending to B: Since A reaches all stations (B, C, D, E), A's transmission interferes with every receiver. No other communication is possible.
  2. Case (b) B sending to A: B's signal is heard by E, A, C (but not D). Thus E or C might try sending to D. However, E and C can reach A, so their transmission would collide with B's signal arriving at receiver A. No other communication is possible.
  3. Case (c) B sending to C: B's signal reaches E, A, C (not D). Station E wants to send to D. Since D is out of range of B, and E is out of range of receiver C, E can safely transmit to D concurrently without interfering with C's reception.

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• (a) A \(\to\) B: None
  • (b) B \(\to\) A: None
  • (c) B \(\to\) C: E can simultaneously transmit to D

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 13]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 11: 802.11b Frame Damage Rate from Bit Error Rate
Problem Statement
docs.text: Suppose an \(11\text{ Mbps}\) 802.11b LAN is transmitting 64-byte frames back-to-back over a radio channel with a Bit Error Rate (BER) of \(p = 10^{-7}\). How many frames per second will be damaged on average?

docs.title: Given Values
docs.text:
• Data rate: \(R = 11\text{ Mbps} = 11 \times 10^6\text{ bps}\)
  • Frame size: \(L = 64\text{ Bytes} = 512\text{ bits}\)
  • Bit Error Rate: \(p = 10^{-7}\)

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Total frames transmitted per second:
\[ N_{\text{fps}} = \f\frac{11 \times 10^6\text{ bps}}{512\text{ bits/frame}} = 21,484.375\text{ frames/sec} \]
  1. Probability that a 512-bit frame arrives with zero bit errors:
\[ P_{\text{correct}} = (1 - p)^{512} = (1 - 10^{-7})^{512} \approx 1 - 512 \times 10^{-7} = 0.9999488 \]
  1. Fraction of damaged frames:
\[ P_{\text{damaged}} = 1 - P_{\text{correct}} \approx 5.12 \times 10^{-5} \]
  1. Damaged frames per second:
\[ \text{Damaged fps} = N_{\text{fps}} \times P_{\text{damaged}} = 21,484 \times (5.12 \times 10^{-5}) \approx 1.10\text{ damaged frames/sec} \approx 1\text{ frame/sec} \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Damaged Frames: \(\approx 1\) damaged frame per second

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 15]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 12: Bluetooth FHSS Dwell Time
Problem Statement
docs.text: Bluetooth uses Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS) with 1600 hops per second across 79 channels. What is the dwell time per frequency hop?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Dwell time is the duration spent on each individual carrier frequency channel:
\[ T_{\text{dwell}} = \f\frac{1}{\text{Hopping Rate}} = \f\frac{1}{1600\text{ hops/sec}} = 0.000625\text{ seconds} = 625\,\mu\text{s} \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Dwell Time: \(625\,\mu\text{s}\)

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 16]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 13: Transparent Bridge Forwarding & Learning Trace
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Two bridges B1 and B2 connect four LAN segments. Initially their hash tables are empty. Ports: * Bridge B1: Port 1 \(\to\) Segment 1 (Hosts A, B); Port 2 \(\to\) Segment 2 (Host C); Port 3 \(\to\) Segment 3 (Host D); Port 4 \(\to\) Link to B2. * Bridge B2: Port 1 \(\to\) Link to B1; Port 2 \(\to\) Segment 4 (Host E); Port 3 \(\to\) Segment 5 (Host F); Port 4 \(\to\) Segment 6 (Host G).

Determine forwarding ports for the following sequence: 1. A sends to C 2. E sends to F 3. F sends to E 4. G sends to E 5. D sends to A 6. B sends to F

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. A \(\to\) C: B1 learns A on Port 1. C unknown \(\implies\) B1 floods to Ports 2, 3, 4. B2 receives on Port 1, learns A on Port 1, floods to Ports 2, 3, 4.
  2. E \(\to\) F: B2 learns E on Port 2. F unknown \(\implies\) B2 floods to Ports 1, 3, 4. B1 receives on Port 4, learns E on Port 4, floods to Ports 1, 2, 3.
  3. F \(\to\) E: B2 learns F on Port 3. E is known on Port 2 \(\implies\) B2 forwards to Port 2 only. B1 does not see this frame.
  4. G \(\to\) E: B2 learns G on Port 4. E is known on Port 2 \(\implies\) B2 forwards to Port 2 only. B1 does not see this frame.
  5. D \(\to\) A: B1 learns D on Port 3. A is known on Port 1 \(\implies\) B1 forwards to Port 1 only. B2 does not see this frame.
  6. B \(\to\) F: B1 learns B on Port 1. F is unknown at B1 \(\implies\) B1 floods to Ports 2, 3, 4. B2 receives on Port 1, knows F on Port 3 \(\implies\) B2 forwards to Port 3 only.

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Page 17]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 14: Intermediate Node Buffer Rate Matching
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Node A sends frames to Node C through intermediate switch B: * Link A \(\to\) B: Distance \(4000\text{ km}\), data rate \(100\text{ kbps}\), sliding window with \(W_s = 3\). * Link B \(\to\) C: Distance \(1000\text{ km}\), stop-and-wait protocol. * Propagation delay: \(5\,\mu\text{s/km}\) on both lines. * Frame size: \(1000\text{ bits}\), ACKs negligible.

Determine the minimum data rate \(R\) required between B and C so that B's buffers do not overflow.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Solution
docs.text:
1. Link A \(\to\) B Analysis:
  2. One-way propagation delay: \(T_{p1} = 4000\text{ km} \times 5\,\mu\text{s/km} = 20\text{ ms}\).
  3. Transmission time per frame: \(T_{t1} = \f\frac{1000\text{ bits}}{100\text{ kbps}} = 10\text{ ms}\).
  4. Frame 1 begins at \(t=0\), finishes sending at \(t=10\text{ ms}\), arrives at B at \(t = 30\text{ ms}\). ACK returns to A at \(t = 50\text{ ms}\).
  5. Sender A transmits 3 frames in 50 ms. Frame arrival rate at B is 3 frames per 50 ms.
  6. Link B \(\to\) C Analysis:
  7. One-way propagation delay: \(T_{p2} = 1000\text{ km} \times 5\,\mu\text{s/km} = 5\text{ ms}\).
  8. Let \(x = \f\frac{1000}{R}\) be the transmission time per frame on link B \(\to\) C.
  9. Total time to send one frame and get ACK: \(T_{\text{cycle}} = x + 2 T_{p2} = x + 10\text{ ms}\).
  10. Time to send 3 frames: \(3(x + 10) = 3x + 30\text{ ms}\).
  11. Equate Frame Inflow and Outflow Rates:
\[ 30 + 3x = 50 \implies 3x = 20 \implies x = \f\frac{20}{3} = 6.667\text{ ms} = 0.006667\text{ s} \]
  1. Calculate minimum data rate \(R\):
\[ R = \f\frac{1000\text{ bits}}{0.006667\text{ s}} = 150,000\text{ bps} = 150\text{ kbps} \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
• Minimum Transmission Rate on Link B \(\to\) C: \(150\text{ kbps}\)

[Source: CN_Numericals_MAC_Layer.pdf, Pages 18–19]

docs.title: 15. Edge Cases, Critical Boundary Conditions & Protocol Anomalies
Edge Case 1: Pure ALOHA Boundary Collisions & Overload Bistability
Boundary Overlap Condition
docs.text: In pure ALOHA, a frame transmitted at time \(t\) has duration \(T_{fr}\). * If another station initiates transmission at \(t - T_{fr} + \epsilon\) (where \(\epsilon > 0\)), its trailing bits collide with the start of the current frame. * If another station initiates transmission at \(t + T_{fr} - \epsilon\), its leading bits collide with the tail of the current frame. * Vulnerable Period: Exactly \(2 T_{fr}\). Even a single bit overlap corrupts both frames entirely due to packet CRC invalidation.

docs.title: The ALOHA Bistability Collapse
docs.text:
Under Poisson arrivals with offered load \(G\):

\[ S = G e^{-2G} \]
  • At low load (\(G < 0.5\)), the system is stable with high throughput.
  • If an accidental traffic burst pushes \(G > 0.5\), collision frequency increases, generating retransmissions.
  • Retransmissions add directly to the offered load, increasing \(G\) further.
  • Higher \(G\) causes more collisions \(\implies\) runaway positive feedback loop where \(G \to \infty\) and useful throughput \(S \to 0\) (complete channel deadlock).

[Source: Ch 4 MAC Layer.pdf, Slides 10–15]

docs.title: Edge Case 2: CSMA/CD \(2\tau\) Collision Window & The Runt Frame Hazard
The \(2\tau\) Vulnerability Window
docs.text: Consider two stations A and B separated by maximum propagation delay \(\tau\): 1. At \(t = 0\), station A senses channel idle and begins transmitting. 2. The wavefront propagates down the cable, reaching station B at \(t = \tau - \epsilon\). 3. At \(t = \tau - \epsilon\), station B has data to send. B senses the cable: the wavefront has not yet arrived! B detects an idle channel and transmits. 4. An immediate collision occurs at \(t = \tau\). 5. Station B detects the collision immediately, aborts, and transmits a 32-bit jam signal. 6. The collision wavefront travels back toward Station A, arriving at Station A at \(t = 2\tau - \epsilon\).

docs.title: Minimum Frame Size Floor Constraint
docs.text:
Station A can only detect collisions while it is actively transmitting bits onto the cable. Therefore:

\[ T_{\text{trans}} \ge 2\tau \implies \frac{L_{\min}}{R} \ge 2\tau \implies L_{\min} \ge 2\tau \cdot R \]

docs.title: The Runt Frame Disaster
docs.text:
If station A transmits a frame of size \(L < L_{\min}\): * Station A finishes sending all bits and clears its transmission buffer before \(t = 2\tau\). * When the collision arrives at \(t = 2\tau - \epsilon\), Station A has already declared the transmission successful! * Station B discards its packet; Station A believes its packet was received; the network is left with a damaged fragment called a runt frame (\(< 64\text{ bytes}\)). This is why Ethernet strictly mandates padding any payload smaller than 46 bytes to enforce a 64-byte minimum frame size.

[Source: Ch 4 MAC Layer.pdf, Slides 42–44]

docs.title: Edge Case 3: Binary Exponential Backoff Capture Effect & 16th Collision Drop
The Capture Effect Anomaly
docs.text: In CSMA/CD, after \(i\) collisions, a station chooses random backoff \(k \in [0, 2^{\min(i, 10)} - 1]\). * Suppose Station A and Station B collide. Both choose from \(\{0, 1\}\). Station A picks 0, transmits successfully. * Station A's collision counter resets to 0. * Station B picks 1, waits, then attempts to transmit. If Station A has another frame, they collide again. * Station A is at its first collision (\(i = 1\), window \(\{0, 1\}\)); Station B is at its second collision (\(i = 2\), window \(\{0, 1, 2, 3\}\)). * Station A has a much higher probability of winning the channel again! * Station A continues to "capture" the physical medium, transmitting consecutive packets while Station B suffers progressive exponential backoff and complete starvation.

docs.title: 16-Collision Hard Abort
docs.text:
If a packet encounters 16 consecutive collisions, the hardware gives up, discards the packet completely, and reports a fatal error to the network layer.

[Source: Ch 4 MAC Layer.pdf, Slide 21]

docs.title: Edge Case 4: Wireless Hidden and Exposed Terminal Dilemmas
1. Hidden Terminal Collision
docs.text:
• Topology: Node A \(\leftrightarrow\) Node B \(\leftrightarrow\) Node C, where A and C cannot detect each other's radio transmissions.
  • Scenario: Both A and C sense the channel idle and transmit to B simultaneously.
  • Result: Colliding signals destroy data at B, even though neither A nor C detected a collision at their own transmitters.
  • Solution: IEEE 802.11 RTS/CTS virtual carrier sensing (NAV).

docs.title: 2. Exposed Terminal Waste
docs.text:
• Topology: Node A \(\leftarrow\) Node B and Node C $ ightarrow$ Node D.
  • Scenario: Node B is transmitting to A. Node C wants to transmit to D.
  • Error: Node C senses B's carrier and defers transmission, fearing a collision.
  • Reality: C transmitting to D would NOT interfere with A receiving from B! The deferral wastes viable radio capacity.

docs.title: 3. RTS Threshold Trade-Off
docs.text:
For small packets, transmitting RTS (20 bytes) + CTS (14 bytes) + ACK (14 bytes) consumes more airtime than the packet itself. Wireless NICs configure an RTS Threshold (typically 2347 bytes): packets below this threshold bypass RTS/CTS and use pure CSMA/CA.

[Source: Ch 4 MAC Layer.pdf, Slide 51]

docs.title: Edge Case 5: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) Convergence Transient Loops
The Layer 2 Loop Catastrophe
docs.text: Unlike IP packets which have a Time-To-Live (TTL) header field that decrements at every hop, Layer 2 Ethernet frames have no TTL field. If a physical loop exists between transparent bridges: * A broadcast frame is flooded onto all ports. * The adjacent bridge receives the broadcast and floods it back onto the first bridge. * The frame circulates endlessly, multiplying exponentially (Broadcast Storm), consuming 100% of link bandwidth and crashing switch CPU processing within seconds.

docs.title: Why STP Listening and Learning States Exist
docs.text:
When STP converges after a topology change, a disabled port must transition through: 1. Blocking \(\to\) Listening (15 s): Port receives BPDUs but transmits no data frames and learns no MAC addresses. 2. Listening \(\to\) Learning (15 s): Port learns MAC addresses from incoming frames to populate its forwarding table, but forwards no data frames. 3. Forwarding: Normal frame transmission begins. The mandatory \(2 \times \text{Forward Delay} = 30\text{ seconds}\) prevents switches with out-of-sync routing databases from forming transient forwarding loops during convergence.

[Source: Ch 4 MAC Layer.pdf, Slides 77–83]

docs.title: Edge Case 6: IEEE 802.1Q Native VLAN & Double Tagging Hopping Attacks
Vulnerability Architecture
docs.text: On an IEEE 802.1Q trunk link, the Native VLAN carries untagged traffic for backward compatibility with legacy hubs. * Double-Tagging Attack Scenario: 1. An attacker on VLAN 10 crafts a frame with two 802.1Q tags: Outer tag = VLAN 10 (native), Inner tag = VLAN 20 (target victim). 2. The frame enters the first switch. The switch strips the outer VLAN 10 tag because VLAN 10 is the native VLAN of the outgoing trunk. 3. The frame traverses the trunk bearing only the inner VLAN 20 tag. 4. The receiving switch inspects the tag, sees VLAN 20, and forwards the packet into the private VLAN 20 broadcast domain!

docs.title: Hardening Rule
docs.text:
Network security standards mandate setting the native VLAN to an unused dummy VLAN ID and explicitly tagging native VLAN traffic on all trunk ports.

[Source: Ch 4 MAC Layer.pdf, Slides 88–89]

docs.title: 16. Connections Between Concepts
docs.text:
• Static FDM/TDM \(\leftrightarrow\) Dynamic Random Access: Burstiness of computer data renders static frequency reservation inefficient (\(N\)-fold delay), leading to dynamic contention and CSMA/CD.
  • CSMA/CD \(\leftrightarrow\) Minimum Frame Sizing: The physical wave speed in copper (\(200\text{ m/}\mu\text{s}\)) directly enforces the 64-byte minimum frame size to guarantee collision detection before transmission ends.
  • Wired vs Wireless MAC: Absence of collision detection in RF channels forces Wi-Fi to abandon CSMA/CD in favor of collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) and virtual carrier sensing (RTS/CTS with NAV).
  • Layer 2 Loops \(\leftrightarrow\) Spanning Tree Protocol: Redundant switch connections ensure fault tolerance but produce broadcast storms; STP dynamically creates a logical loop-free tree while preserving physical redundancy.
  • VLANs \(\leftrightarrow\) Broadcast Domains: VLANs utilize 802.1Q tagging to partition single physical switches into isolated broadcast domains, eliminating the need for separate physical switch hardware.

docs.title: 17. Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. The MAC sublayer resolves channel contention across shared broadcast media.
  2. Pure ALOHA achieves \(18.4\%\) max throughput (\(S = G e^{-2G}\)); Slotted ALOHA doubles throughput to \(36.8\%\) (\(S = G e^{-G}\)).
  3. CSMA senses the carrier before sending. CSMA/CD detects collisions during transmission and aborts, using Binary Exponential Backoff.
  4. Ethernet minimum frame size (\(64\text{ Bytes}\)) is mathematically required to cover the round-trip contention window (\(2\tau = 51.2\,\mu\text{s}\)).
  5. Wireless LANs suffer from Hidden and Exposed terminal problems; IEEE 802.11 resolves them using CSMA/CA, RTS/CTS handshakes, and NAV timers.
  6. Transparent bridges use backward learning to forward frames based on destination MAC addresses.
  7. Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D) prevents broadcast storms by disabling redundant bridge links into a blocking state.
  8. IEEE 802.1Q inserts 4-byte tags into Ethernet frames across trunk links to segment traffic into up to 4094 logical VLANs.

docs.title: 3. Collision Probability in Slotted Broadcast
docs.text: \[ P_{\text{collision}} = 1 - n p(1-p)^{n-1} - (1-p)^n \]

docs.title: 4. Optimal Contention Probability
docs.text: \[ p^* = \f\frac{1}{k} \implies P_{\max} = \left(1 - \f\frac{1}{k}\r\right)^{k-1} \to \f\frac{1}{e} \approx 36.8\% \]

docs.title: 5. CSMA/CD Minimum Frame Size
docs.text: \[ L_{\min} = 2 \cdot \tau \cdot B = 2 \cdot \left(\f\frac{D}{v}\r\right) \cdot B \]

docs.title: 6. Ethernet Channel Efficiency
docs.text: \[ \eta = \f\frac{1}{1 + \f\frac{2 B L e}{c F}} \]

docs.title: 7. Bit-Map Protocol Overhead & Efficiency
docs.text: \[ \text{Efficiency}_{\text{low}} = \f\frac{d}{d + N}, \quad \text{Efficiency}_{\text{high}} = \f\frac{d}{d + 1} \]

docs.title: 8. Binary Countdown Overhead & Efficiency
docs.text: \[ \text{Efficiency} = \f\frac{d}{d + \log_2 N} \]

docs.title: 19. Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Medium Access Control (MAC): Lower sublayer of Layer 2 that determines which station transmits on a shared channel.
  • Collision: Destructive interference when two or more frames overlap on a broadcast channel.
  • Vulnerable Period: Time window where a frame is susceptible to colliding with another frame.
  • Offered Load (\(G\)): Total frame transmission attempts per frame time.
  • CSMA/CD: Access method that senses carrier and aborts immediately upon detecting collision.
  • Binary Exponential Backoff: Delay algorithm that exponentially expands random backoff range after successive collisions.
  • Hidden Terminal: Station whose wireless transmissions interfere at a receiver without being heard by other senders.
  • Network Allocation Vector (NAV): Virtual carrier-sensing timer indicating channel busy duration in Wi-Fi.
  • Transparent Bridge: Layer 2 forwarding switch that automatically learns station locations from source MACs.
  • Spanning Tree Protocol: Algorithm that prunes redundant bridged topologies into a loop-free tree.
  • VLAN: Logical broadcast domain configured within switch software, tagged via 802.1Q.

docs.title: Important Concepts for Examinations
docs.text:
1. ALOHA Derivations: Recreate throughput equations \(S = G e^{-2G}\) and \(S = G e^{-G}\); calculate vulnerable periods and peak capacities.
  2. CSMA/CD & Frame Size: Derive \(L_{\min} = 2\tau B\); explain the physical mechanism behind the 64-byte minimum Ethernet frame size.
  3. 802.11 MAC & CSMA/CA: Compare CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA; draw RTS/CTS timing diagrams with SIFS/DIFS and explain NAV virtual carrier sensing.
  4. Transparent Bridge Learning: Trace bridge forwarding tables step-by-step for incoming frame sequences (Filter, Forward, Flood).
  5. Spanning Tree Algorithm: Elect Root Bridge (lowest BID), Root Ports, and Designated Ports on network topologies.
  6. VLAN Tagging (802.1Q): Identify TPID, Priority (802.1p), and 12-bit VID fields; explain Access vs Trunk ports.

docs.title: Extracted Official Question Bank & Tutorial Problems with Solutions
Q1. Which device primarily operates at the Data Link Layer to segment collision domains?
docs.text:
• Options: A. Router | B. Hub | C. Switch (Bridge) | D. Gateway
  • Answer: C. Switch

docs.title: Q2. What is the access method used in standard Ethernet?
docs.text:
• Options: A. Token Passing | B. CSMA/CD | C. FDMA | D. TDMA
  • Answer: B. CSMA/CD

docs.title: Q3. In CSMA/CD, if propagation delay is \(15\,\mu\text{s}\), what is the worst-case time to detect a collision?
docs.text:
• Given: \(\tau = 15\,\mu\text{s}\).
  • Calculation:
\[ \text{Worst-case Detection Time} = 2\tau = 2 \times 15\,\mu\text{s} = 30\,\mu\text{s} \]

docs.title: Q4. An Ethernet LAN transmits data at \(1\text{ Gbps}\). Calculate the amount of data transmitted in 2 seconds.
docs.text:
• Calculation:
\[ \text{Data} = 10^9\text{ bps} \times 2\text{ s} = 2 \times 10^9\text{ bits} = 2\text{ Gb} = 250\text{ MB} \]

docs.title: Q5. A slotted ALOHA system has a \(40\%\) probability of successful transmission in a slot. Calculate channel throughput.
docs.text: • Answer: Throughput \(S = 0.40\) (\(40\%\) channel capacity utilized).

docs.title: Q6. What is the maximum number of VLANs supported by IEEE 802.1Q standard?
docs.text:
• Calculation: The VLAN ID field is 12 bits wide \(\implies 2^{12} = 4096\) total (\(1\) to \(4094\) usable).

[Source: Computer_Networks_Question_Bank.pdf, Unit 3, Q21–Q41; cn_tutorial.pdf, Tutorial 4]

docs.title: 1.1 What is a Computer Network?
docs.text: • Faculty Definition: A computer network is a set of autonomous computers interconnected by a single technology to share resources, exchange data, and facilitate communication. [Faculty — Slide 2] • General / Reference Definition: A computer network is an interconnected collection of autonomous computers. Two computers are said to be interconnected if they are able to exchange information. The connection need not be via a copper wire; fiber optics, microwaves, infrared, and communication satellites can also be used. [General — Slide 2] • Key Terminologies: • Node: Any device (e.g., computer, printer, router, switch) capable of sending and/or receiving data generated by other nodes on the network. [Faculty + General] • Communication Link: The physical or wireless medium (e.g., coaxial cable, twisted pair, optical fiber, radio waves) connecting nodes. [Faculty + General] • Autonomous: A computer is autonomous if it can function independently without master-slave control by another computer. A system with one control computer and multiple slave terminals is not a computer network. [General — Slide 2]

docs.title: 1.2 Computer Networks vs. Distributed Systems
docs.text:
Feature Computer Network Distributed System User Visibility Existence of autonomous machines is explicit and Existence of multiple autonomous computers is hidden visible to the user. User must log in remotely or (transparent). The system appears as a single unified explicitly transfer files. system to the user. Control / OS Each machine runs its own local operating system. A global software layer (middleware / distributed OS) manages resources across nodes seamlessly. Examples The World Wide Web, local office network. Distributed database, World Wide Web with automated middleware / cloud compute cluster.

[Faculty — Slide 3 / General — Slide 2]

docs.title: 1.3 Core Characteristics of Computer Networks
docs.text:
1. Fault Tolerance: The network must route traffic around failed hardware or links so that failure of a single node or link does not bring down overall communication. [Faculty — Slide 4]
  2. Scalability: The ability of the network to expand efficiently (adding new nodes, networks, and services) without suffering severe performance degradation. [Faculty — Slide 4]
  3. Quality of Service (QoS): The capability of a network to provide better service to selected network traffic over various technologies (managing delay, jitter, throughput, and packet loss). [Faculty — Slide 4]
  4. Security: Protecting network assets and data against unauthorized access, corruption, or interception (ensuring Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability - CIA). [Faculty — Slide 4] ──────

docs.title: 2. Uses and Applications of Computer Networks
2.1 Business Applications
docs.text:
• Resource Sharing: Making programs, equipment (printers, storage), and data available to anyone on the network regardless of physical location. [Faculty + General — Slide 5] • Client-Server Model: • Data is stored on central computers called Servers. • Employees (users) access data via remote machines called Clients. • Communication follows a Request-Reply paradigm: Client sends a request over the network; Server processes it and returns a reply. [Faculty — Slide 6-7 / General — Slide 6-7]

  +------------------+                    +------------------+
  |   Client Machine |                    |   Server Machine |
  |   +------------+ |    Request Frame   | +--------------+ |
  |   | Process 1  | | ==================>| | Server Proc  | |
  |   +------------+ | <==================| +--------------+ |
  |                  |    Reply Frame     |                  |
  +------------------+                    +------------------+

[Diagram: Client-Server Architecture — Faculty Slide 7]

• IP Telephony / VoIP: Voice over IP allows business phone systems to operate over standard IP network cables rather than separate telephone wiring. [Faculty — Slide 7] • Virtual Private Networks (VPNs): Securely joins separate physical locations of an enterprise into a single logical network over the public Internet. [Faculty + General — Slide 21] • E-Commerce: Buying, selling, and executing business transactions electronically over the network. [General — Slide 9] ──────

docs.title: 2.2 Home Applications
docs.text:
• Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Architecture: There are no fixed, dedicated servers or clients. Every node (peer) can act as both client and server, sharing resources directly (e.g., BitTorrent, IPFS). [Faculty — Slide 8 / General — Slide 8]

  +--------+              +--------+
  | Peer A |<------------>| Peer B |
  +--------+              +--------+
      ^                       ^
      |                       |
      v                       v
  +--------+              +--------+
  | Peer C |<------------>| Peer D |
  +--------+              +--------+

[Diagram: Peer-to-Peer Model — Faculty Slide 8]

docs.title: Person-to-Person Communication
docs.text: • Email, instant messaging, video calls, social networking, and user-generated content (wikis, blogs). [General — Slide 8]

docs.title: Entertainment & Media
docs.text: • On-demand video streaming (Netflix, YouTube), online multiplayer gaming, IPTV. [General — Slide 8]

docs.title: E-Commerce Categories
docs.text:
• B2C (Business-to-Consumer): Online ordering of products (e.g., Amazon).
  • B2B (Business-to-Business): Businesses purchasing raw materials from suppliers.
  • C2C (Consumer-to-Consumer): Individuals selling products/services to other individuals (e.g., eBay).
  • G2C (Government-to-Consumer): Government-provided services (e.g., tax filing portals).
  • C2B (Consumer-to-Business): Consumers listing budgets for services, and businesses bidding for them. [Faculty — Slide 9 / General — Slide 9]

docs.title: Mobile Computing vs. Wireless Communication
docs.text:
• Mobile Wireless: Laptops/smartphones connected through 4G/5G/Wi-Fi while moving.
  • Fixed Wireless: Desktop PCs connected via wireless links within a building.
  • Mobile Wired: Laptop connected to an Ethernet jack at different locations (e.g., hotel desks).
  • Fixed Wired: Desktop PC permanently connected through wired networks in an office. [Faculty — Slide 10 / General — Slide 10]

docs.title: Wearable Devices & Sensor Networks
docs.text: • Examples include smartwatches, environmental sensors, and medical monitoring implants. [Faculty — Slide 49]

docs.title: Network Neutrality
docs.text: • The principle that Internet Service Providers (ISPs) must treat all Internet data equally, without discriminating or charging differently based on users, content, websites, platforms, or applications. [Faculty — Slide 11 / General — Slide 11]

docs.title: Privacy, Freedom of Speech, Censorship, and Copyright
docs.text: • These involve conflicts between copyright holders, state censorship, user anonymity, and wiretapping laws. [Faculty — Slide 11 / General — Slide 11]

docs.title: A. Broadcast Links
docs.text:
• A single communication channel is shared by all machines on the network. • Packets sent by any machine are received by all machines on the network. • An address field inside the packet header specifies the intended recipient. • Nodes inspect the destination address: if addressed to them, they process it; otherwise, they ignore it. [Faculty — Slide 13 / General — Slide 13]

Addressing Modes in Broadcast Networks:

  1. Unicast: Packet intended for exactly one node.
  2. Multicast: Packet intended for a subset of nodes (indicated by a special multicast bit/address).
  3. Broadcast: Packet intended for all nodes on the network (indicated by a reserved broadcast address, e.g., all 1s in binary). [Faculty — Slide 15 / General — Slide 15]

docs.title: B. Point-to-Point Links
docs.text: • Consists of many connections between individual pairs of machines. • To go from source to destination, a packet may have to visit one or more intermediate nodes. • Routing algorithms are required to find optimal paths through the network. • Generally used in larger, wide-area networks (WANs). [Faculty — Slide 14 / General — Slide 14] ──────

docs.title: Detailed Breakdown of Scale Architectures:
docs.text:
1. PAN (Personal Area Network): • Operates over short ranges (around 1 m to 10 m). • Uses technologies like Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1) or Zigbee (802.15.4) in master-slave configurations. [Faculty — Slide 17]
  2. LAN (Local Area Network): • Privately owned networks operating within a single building or campus. • Wired LANs: Use point-to-point links connected via a central Switch (Switched Ethernet, IEEE 802.3). • Wireless LANs (WLANs): Use radio signals broadcast from an Access Point (AP) (IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi). [Faculty — Slide 18]
  3. MAN (Metropolitan Area Network): • Covers an entire city. • Classic example: Cable Television networks upgraded to convey two-way Internet data (DOCSIS standards). [Faculty — Slide 19]
  4. WAN (Wide Area Network): • Spans large geographical areas (countries/continents). • Consists of two distinct elements: • Hosts: Customer machines executing user applications. • Subnet / Network Core: Connects hosts. Consists of Transmission Lines (copper/fiber/radios) and Routers (switching elements that connect two or more transmission lines). [Faculty — Slide 20 / General — Slide 20-22]

docs.title: 3.3 Key Hardware & Switching Terms
docs.text: • Packet: A discrete block of data containing a header (control info, addresses) and payload (actual data). [General — Slide 23] • Packet Switching: Transmission technique where data stream is divided into packets that are routed independently across shared network links. [General — Slide 23] • Circuit Switching: A dedicated physical path (circuit) is established between sender and receiver for the entire duration of the call (e.g., traditional telephone network). [Faculty — Slide 43] • Datagram: A connectionless packet transfer mechanism where each packet carries full source and destination addresses and is routed independently. [General — Slide 23] • Virtual Circuit: A connection-oriented packet switching technique where a pre-planned logical path is established through routers before data packets are sent. [General — Slide 23] ──────

docs.title: 4.1 Protocol Hierarchies
docs.text:
To reduce design complexity, most networks are organized as a stack of layers or levels, each built upon the one below it.

• Layer: A module designed to perform a specific abstraction or task. [Faculty + General — Slide 24] • Protocol: An agreement/set of rules between the communicating parties (peer entities) on how communication is to take place across a layer. [Faculty + General — Slide 24-25] • Interface: Defines which primitive operations and services the lower layer offers to the layer directly above it. [Faculty + General — Slide 25] • Network Architecture: A set of layers and protocols. The specification of the architecture must contain enough information to allow an implementer to write the software or build the hardware for each layer. [Faculty + General — Slide 25] • Protocol Stack: The specific list of protocols used by a system, one protocol per layer. [Faculty + General — Slide 25] ──────

docs.title: 4.2 The Philosopher-Translator-Secretary Analogy
docs.text:
To visualize layered communication:

• Two philosophers (Layer 3 entities) in different countries want to communicate. Philosopher 1 speaks Swahili; Philosopher 2 speaks French. • Philosopher 1 passes his message to a Translator (Layer 2 entity), who translates it to English (an agreed protocol). • The Translator passes the English message to a Secretary (Layer 1 entity), who sends it via Fax/Email (Physical medium). • At the destination, the Secretary receives the raw fax, hands it to the Translator (who translates English to French), who hands the French message to Philosopher 2.

  +------------------+                          +------------------+
  | Philosopher (L3) | <--- Virtual Protocol--> | Philosopher (L3) |
  +--------+---------+                          +--------+---------+
           | Interface                                   | Interface
  +--------v---------+                          +--------v---------+
  | Translator  (L2) | <--- Virtual Protocol--> | Translator  (L2) |
  +--------+---------+                          +--------+---------+
           | Interface                                   | Interface
  +--------v---------+                          +--------v---------+
  | Secretary   (L1) | <--- Virtual Protocol--> | Secretary   (L1) |
  +--------+---------+                          +--------+---------+
           | Physical Medium                             | Physical Medium
  +--------v---------------------------------------------v---------+
  |                    Physical Communication Path                  |
  +-----------------------------------------------------------------+

[Diagram: Virtual vs Actual Layered Communication — Faculty Slide 26] ──────

• This process is called Encapsulation. • At the receiving host, as data moves up the stack, headers are stripped off layer-by-layer ( Decapsulation). [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: 4.4 Major Layer Design Issues
docs.text:
1. Addressing: Identifying senders and receivers across layers.
  2. Error Control: Detecting and correcting bit errors introduced by physical links.
  3. Flow Control: Preventing a fast sender from swamping a slow receiver.
  4. Multiplexing & Demultiplexing: Combining multiple upper-layer conversations onto a single lower-layer channel, and separating them at the destination.
  5. Routing: Choosing optimal paths through a mesh of intermediate routers.
  6. Scalability & Security: Ensuring performance holds as network grows, and preventing tampering/eavesdropping. [Faculty — Slide 24 / General — Slide 24] ──────

docs.title: 5.1 Detailed Breakdown
docs.text:
Services
                                |
        +-----------------------+-----------------------+
        |                                               |
Connection-Oriented                             Connectionless
(Telephone Model)                               (Postal Mail Model)
  1. Setup Connection                             1. Packets sent independently
  2. Use Connection                               2. No setup / teardown
  3. Release Connection                           3. Packets may arrive out-of-order
  1. Connection-Oriented Service: • Patterned after the telephone system. • Requires establishing a connection prior to sending data, using it for data transfer, and tearing it down afterwards. • Acts like a pipe: sender pushes bits in at one end, receiver extracts them in the exact same order at the other end. [Faculty + General — Slide 28]
  2. Connectionless Service: • Patterned after the postal system. • Each message (datagram) carries the full destination address and is routed independently through the intermediate nodes. • Later-sent packets may arrive before earlier-sent packets (out-of-order delivery). [Faculty + General — Slide 28]

──────

docs.text:
Service Category Service Type Standard Example / Analogy Connection-Oriented Reliable Message Stream Sequence of discrete pages/documents Reliable Byte Stream Movie streaming, file transfer (TCP) Unreliable Connection Digitized voice / IP Telephony Connectionless Unreliable Datagram Electronic junk mail, UDP Acknowledged Datagram Registered mail with return receipt Request-Reply Client-server database query

[Faculty — Slide 28 / General — Slide 28] ──────

docs.title: 6.1 Service vs. Protocol (Crucial Distinction)
docs.text:
• Service: A set of primitive operations that a lower layer provides to the layer above it. The service defines what operations the layer is prepared to perform, but says nothing about how these operations are implemented (Vertical Interface abstraction). [Faculty + General — Slide 31] • Protocol: A set of rules governing the format and meaning of frames, packets, or messages that are exchanged between peer entities within the same layer across different machines (Horizontal Interaction). [Faculty + General — Slide 31]

  Host A (Layer N+1)                             Host B (Layer N+1)
      |                                              ^
      | Service Primitive                            | Service Primitive
      v (Vertical)                                   | (Vertical)
  Host A (Layer N)   <===== Layer N Protocol =====>  Host B (Layer N)
                              (Horizontal)
──────

docs.title: 6.2 The Six Core Service Primitives
docs.text:
For a simple connection-oriented service:

Primitive Type Meaning / Action LISTEN Passive Block waiting for an incoming connection request CONNECT Active Establish a connection by sending a request packet ACCEPT Active Accept an incoming connection request RECEIVE Passive Block waiting for an incoming data packet SEND Active Send a data packet to the peer entity DISCONNECT Active Terminate / release the connection

[Faculty — Slide 29 / General — Slide 29] ──────

docs.title: 6.3 Sequence of Primitives in Client-Server Communication
docs.text:
Client Host                                   Server Host
   +---------------+                             +---------------+
   |               |                             | Exec `LISTEN` |
   |               |                             | (Blocks)      |
   | Exec `CONNECT`| -- (1) Connect Request -->  |               |
   | (Blocks)      |                             | Unblocks      |
   |               | <- (2) Connect Ack/Accept-- | Exec `ACCEPT` |
   | Unblocks      |                             | Exec `RECEIVE`|
   | Exec `SEND`   | -- (3) Data Request ------> | (Blocks)      |
   | Exec `RECEIVE`|                             | Process Data  |
   | (Blocks)      | <- (4) Data Reply -------- | Exec `SEND`   |
   | Exec `DISCONN`| -- (5) Disconnect Req --->  | Exec `DISCONN`|
   +---------------+                             +---------------+

[Diagram: Client-Server Interaction via Primitives — General Slide 30] ──────

docs.title: 7.1 The OSI Reference Model (7 Layers)
docs.text: Developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). [Faculty + General — Slide 32-35]

docs.title: ISO OSI Principles for Layering:
docs.text:
1. A layer should be created where a different abstraction is needed.
  2. Each layer should perform a well-defined function.
  3. The function of each layer should be chosen with an eye toward defining internationally standardized protocols.
  4. Layer boundaries should be chosen to minimize information flow across interfaces. [General — Slide 33]
+-----------------------------------+
| 7. Application Layer              |
+-----------------------------------+
| 6. Presentation Layer             |
+-----------------------------------+
| 5. Session Layer                  |
+-----------------------------------+
| 4. Transport Layer                |  <-- End-to-End Control
+-----------------------------------+
| 3. Network Layer                  |  <-- Subnet Routing
+-----------------------------------+
| 2. Data Link Layer                |  <-- Node-to-Node Hop
+-----------------------------------+
| 1. Physical Layer                 |  <-- Bit Stream Transmission
+-----------------------------------+

docs.title: Functions of the 7 OSI Layers:
docs.text:
1. Physical Layer (Layer 1): Transmits raw bits over a communication channel. Defines voltage levels, bit timing, pin counts, and transmission media specs. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  2. Data Link Layer (Layer 2): Takes raw transmission facility and transforms it into a line that appears free of undetected transmission errors. Groups bits into frames, handles frame synchronization, error detection/correction, and flow control. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  3. Network Layer (Layer 3): Controls the operation of the subnet. Handles packet routing, congestion control, and internetworking between heterogeneous networks. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  4. Transport Layer (Layer 4): Accepts data from Session layer, splits it up into smaller units, passes these to Network layer, and ensures that all pieces arrive correctly at the other end. True end-to-end layer. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  5. Session Layer (Layer 5): Allows users on different machines to establish sessions between them. Provides dialog control (keeping track of whose turn it is to transmit) and synchronization (inserting checkpoints into long transfers). [Faculty — Slide 35 / General — Slide 57]
  6. Presentation Layer (Layer 6): Concerned with the syntax and semantics of the information transmitted. Handles data format conversions, encoding, data compression, and encryption. [Faculty — Slide 35 / General — Slide 57]
  7. Application Layer (Layer 7): Contains a variety of protocols that users commonly need (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS). [Faculty — Slide 35] ──────

docs.title: Functions of the TCP/IP Layers:
docs.text:
1. Link Layer (Host-to-Network): Describes what links (such as serial lines or Ethernet) must do to meet the needs of the connectionless Internet layer. It is not really a layer in the strict sense, but an interface between hosts and transmission links. [General — Slide 36]
  2. Internet Layer: The linchpin of the architecture. Defines an official packet format and protocol called IP (Internet Protocol). Routes IP packets to their destinations independently. Handles packet delivery across network boundaries. [General — Slide 36]
  3. Transport Layer: Allows peer entities on the source and destination hosts to carry on a conversation. • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Reliable connection-oriented, byte-stream protocol. Provides flow control and congestion control. • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Unreliable connectionless datagram protocol for applications that prefer low latency over reliability. [General — Slide 36]
  4. Application Layer: Contains all higher-level protocols (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, DNS). [General — Slide 36] ──────

docs.title: 7.3 The Hybrid 5-Layer Model (Used in Textbook & Course)
docs.text:
Combines the features of OSI and TCP/IP for pedagogical clarity: [Faculty — Slide 39 / General — Slide 39]

  5-Layer Hybrid Model
  +------------------------+
  | 5. Application Layer   |
  +------------------------+
  | 4. Transport Layer     |
  +------------------------+
  | 3. Network Layer       |
  +------------------------+
  | 2. Data Link Layer     |
  +------------------------+
  | 1. Physical Layer      |
  +------------------------+
──────

docs.title: 7.4 Detailed Comparison: OSI vs. TCP/IP Models
docs.text:
Feature / Property OSI Model TCP/IP Model Number of Layers 7 Layers 4 Layers Service vs Protocol Distinction Explicitly distinguished. Services, Implicitly merged. Distinctions are blurry; Interfaces, and Protocols are clear. protocols fit loosely. Development Approach Model was devised before protocols were Protocols were written first; model was a written (Theoretical). description of existing protocols (Practical). Network Layer Communication Supports both Connection-Oriented and Supports only Connectionless communication Connectionless communication. (IP). Transport Layer Communication Supports only Connection-Oriented Supports both Connection-Oriented (TCP) and communication. Connectionless (UDP). Session & Presentation Layers Present as separate, explicit layers (5 & Omitted entirely / integrated into 6). Application layer. Physical & Data Link Layers Explicitly separated into Layers 1 and 2. Combined into a single "Link" or "Host-to- Network" layer.

[Faculty — Slide 40 / General — Slide 40] ──────

docs.title: A. Critique of the OSI Model ("The Four Bads") [Faculty + General — Slide 41]
docs.text:
1. Bad Timing: The OSI standards were published after TCP/IP was already heavily deployed in universities and industry ( The "Elephant Problem": TCP/IP took over the market before OSI was finalized).
  2. Bad Technology: Session and Presentation layers are virtually empty; Data Link and Physical layers are heavily redundant; complex and inefficient implementation.
  3. Bad Implementation: Initial OSI implementations were slow, bulky, and buggy compared to TCP/IP.
  4. Bad Politics: OSI was seen as government/telecom bureaucrat-driven, while TCP/IP was seen as open-source academic hacker- driven.

docs.title: B. Critique of the TCP/IP Model
docs.text:
1. Does not clearly distinguish between concepts of service, interface, and protocol.
  2. Not general; hard to adapt to describe protocol stacks other than TCP/IP.
  3. The Link layer is not really a layer in the architectural sense, but an interface.
  4. Completely omits physical and data link layer specifications. [General — Slide 41] ──────

docs.title: 8.1 ARPANET History & Paul Baran's Innovation
docs.text:
• In the 1960s, the US Defense Department wanted a command-and-control network that could survive a nuclear strike. • Centralized / Hierarchical Networks (Telephone System): Vulnerable because destruction of a single central switch breaks communication for all connected nodes. • Paul Baran's Distributed Packet Switching: Proposed a mesh network of interconnected switching nodes (IMPs - Interface Message Processors). Packets dynamically route around destroyed nodes. [Faculty — Slide 42-43 / General — Slide 43-46]

   (a) Centralized                    (b) Distributed Mesh (Baran)
       [Switch]                             (O)-----(O)-----(O)
      /   |    \                            | \     / |     / |
   (O)   (O)   (O)                          |  (O)----(O)---- |
                                            (O)------------- (O)

[Diagram: Centralized Telephone System vs Baran's Distributed Network — General Slide 43] ──────

docs.title: 8.3 Wireless LANs (IEEE 802.11)
docs.text:
• Infrastructure Mode: Wireless hosts connect to a wired network via a central Access Point ( AP). [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 49] • Ad-hoc Mode: Computers connect directly peer-to-peer without an AP. [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 49] • Wireless Transmission Challenges: • Multipath Fading: Signals reflect off walls/obstacles, arriving at the receiver out of phase and causing signal cancellation. [Faculty — Slide 47 / General — Slide 50] • Hidden Terminal Problem: Transmitters out of radio range of each other cause collisions at an intermediate receiver. [General — Slide 51]

──────

docs.title: 9.1 Key Standards Organizations
docs.text:
1. ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union - Telecommunication Standardization Sector): UN specialized agency for telecommunications standards. [Faculty — Slide 50]
  2. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers): Develops local and metropolitan area network standards ( IEEE 802 committee). [Faculty — Slide 50]
  3. IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force): Publishes RFCs (Requests for Comments) defining Internet protocols (IP, TCP, HTTP). [Faculty — Slide 50]
  4. ISO (International Organization for Standardization): Formulated the OSI model. [Faculty — Slide 50] ──────

docs.title: 10.1 Speed & Bandwidth Prefixes (Base 10)
docs.text:
In networking communications, speed, data rate, and bandwidth use Powers of 10 (10³):

\[ 1 \text{ Kbps} = 10^3 \text{ bits/sec} = 1,000 \text{ bps} \] \[ 1 \text{ Mbps} = 10^6 \text{ bits/sec} = 1,000,000 \text{ bps} \] \[ 1 \text{ Gbps} = 10^9 \text{ bits/sec} = 1,000,000,000 \text{ bps} \]

[Faculty — Slide 51 / General — Slide 55]

docs.title: 10.2 Storage & Memory Prefixes (Base 2)
docs.text:
Data storage (RAM, Disk sizes) uses Powers of 2 (2¹⁰):

\[ 1 \text{ KB} = 2^{10} \text{ bytes} = 1,024 \text{ bytes} \] \[ 1 \text{ MB} = 2^{20} \text{ bytes} = 1,048,576 \text{ bytes} \] \[ 1 \text{ GB} = 2^{30} \text{ bytes} = 1,073,741,824 \text{ bytes} \]

[Faculty — Slide 51 / General — Slide 55]

docs.title: 10.3 Time Prefixes
docs.text:
\[ 1 \text{ millisecond (ms)} = 10^{-3} \text{ seconds} \] \[ 1 \text{ microsecond (\mu s)} = 10^{-6} \text{ seconds} \] \[ 1 \text{ nanosecond (ns)} = 10^{-9} \text{ seconds} \]

[Faculty — Slide 51 / General — Slide 56]

docs.title: 11.1 Complete Formula Sheet
docs.text:
1. Network Metric Conversion (Bandwidth vs Storage): • Transmission Speed: 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits/sec • Memory Storage: 1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes = 1,048,576 bytes

──────

docs.title: 11.2 Important Definitions
docs.text: • Computer Network: A collection of autonomous computers interconnected by communication links to exchange information. • Protocol: Rules governing the format and meaning of messages exchanged between peer entities at the same layer. • Service: Operations a lower layer provides to the layer directly above it via an interface. • Encapsulation: Adding layer headers/trailers to higher-layer SDUs as data moves down the stack. • Network Neutrality: Treating all Internet data traffic equally without discrimination by source, content, or application. ──────

docs.title: 11.3 Important Comparisons
docs.text: • Computer Network vs Distributed System: Explicit node visibility vs transparent unified system. • OSI vs TCP/IP: 7 layers vs 4 layers; theory-driven vs practical-driven; strict service/protocol separation vs merged concept. • Connection-Oriented vs Connectionless: Dedicated setup phase / in-order delivery vs independent datagram routing / possible reordering. ──────

docs.title: 11.4 Exam Revision Notes
docs.text: • Must-Know Diagrams: OSI 7-layer model, TCP/IP 4-layer model, Client-Server architecture, Encapsulation flow down stack. • Must-Know Concepts: Distinction between Service (vertical interface) and Protocol (horizontal peer rule). • Commonly Confused Prefixes: 1 Mbps in transmission bandwidth is 10⁶ bits/s, NOT 2²⁰. ──────────── Chapter 3 — Data Link Layer ──────

docs.title: 1.1 Role and Core Objectives of Data Link Layer
docs.text: • The Physical Layer delivers raw bits over a physical medium. However, physical channels suffer from: • Limited bandwidth • Signal distortions and bit errors • Propagation delays [Faculty — Slide 3] • Primary Objective of Data Link Layer: To transform a raw transmission facility into a line that appears free of undetected transmission errors to the Network Layer above it. [Faculty — Slide 4] ──────

docs.title: 1.2 Functions of Data Link Layer
docs.text:
1. Providing a well-defined service interface to the Network Layer.
  2. Framing: Grouping physical bit streams into discrete units called frames.
  3. Error Handling: Detecting and correcting errors (corrupted, lost, or duplicate frames).
  4. Flow Control: Regulating data transmission rate so fast senders do not overwhelm slow receivers. [Faculty — Slide 4] ──────

docs.title: 1.3 Layer Relationship & Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
• Virtual vs. Actual Communication: The Data Link Layer entities communicate virtually via a Data Link Protocol, but actual data flows down to the Physical Layer, across the physical medium, and back up. [Faculty — Slide 6 / General — Slide 9]

  Host A (Network Layer)                           Host B (Network Layer)
            |                                                ^
            v Virtual Data Link Protocol Path                |
  Host A (Data Link Layer) =====================> Host B (Data Link Layer)
            |                                                ^
            v Actual Physical Transmission Path              |
  Host A (Physical Layer)  ---------------------> Host B (Physical Layer)

• Hardware vs. Software Implementation: • NIC (Network Interface Card): Handles Physical Layer processes and time-critical Data Link Layer functions (framing, CRC hardware check, bit stuffing). • OS Kernel Device Driver: Handles higher link-layer logic, software timers, and Network Layer interactions on the main CPU. [Faculty — Slide 34 / General — Slide 32]

──────

docs.title: 1.4 Services Offered to Network Layer
docs.text:
1. Unacknowledged Connectionless Service: • Source sends independent frames without destination acknowledging them. • No connection setup or release. • Lost frames are not recovered by the link layer. • Use Cases: Low error rate channels (copper LANs) or real-time voice traffic where delay is worse than lost frames. [Faculty — Slide 8 / General — Slide 11]
  2. Acknowledged Connectionless Service: • Source sends independent frames, but each frame is individually acknowledged by the receiver. • If a frame does not arrive within a timeout period, it is retransmitted. • Use Cases: Highly unreliable wireless links (e.g., IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi). [Faculty — Slide 9 / General — Slide 12]
  3. Acknowledged Connection-Oriented Service: • Connection is established before any data is sent. • Frames are numbered, acknowledged, and guaranteed to arrive exactly once and in the correct order. • Three Phases: Connection Establishment → Data Transfer → Connection Release. • Use Cases: Long-distance point-to-point satellite channels. [Faculty — Slide 10 / General — Slide 13]

──────

docs.title: 2.1 Why Framing is Necessary
docs.text: Physical Layer delivers a continuous stream of raw bits. To detect and recover from errors, the stream must be broken down into discrete Frames, so checksums can be computed for each frame. [Faculty — Slide 11 / General — Slide 14] ──────

docs.title: Method 1: Character Count / Byte Count
docs.text:
• Uses a field in the frame header to specify the total number of characters/bytes in the frame. • Mechanism: Receiver reads the count field to know where the frame ends. [Faculty — Slide 12 / General — Slide 15]

  Frame 1 (5 bytes)     Frame 2 (5 bytes)     Frame 3 (8 bytes)
  +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
  | 5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | | 5 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | | 8 | 9 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
  +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+

• Fatal Flaw / Disadvantage: If a single bit error corrupts the count field (e.g., a 5 becomes a 7), the receiver loses frame synchronization completely and cannot locate the start of subsequent frames. [Faculty — Slide 12 / General — Slide 16] ──────

docs.title: Method 2: Flag Bytes with Byte Stuffing (Character Stuffing)
docs.text:
• Delimits frames with special control bytes called FLAG bytes (e.g., ASCII DLE STX / DLE ETX or 0x7E). • Problem: What if the binary payload data itself contains the byte value matching FLAG? • Byte Stuffing Rule: • Sender inserts a special Escape byte (ESC) (e.g., 0x7D) immediately before any instance of FLAG or ESC occurring within the payload. • Receiver strips off the ESC byte upon reception. [Faculty — Slide 13-16 / General — Slide 17-19]

  Original Payload:       [ A ] [ FLAG ] [ B ]
  Transmitted (Stuffed):  [ FLAG ] [ A ] [ ESC ] [ FLAG ] [ B ] [ FLAG ]

  Original Payload:       [ A ] [ ESC ] [ B ]
  Transmitted (Stuffed):  [ FLAG ] [ A ] [ ESC ] [ ESC ] [ B ] [ FLAG ]
──────

docs.title: Method 3: Flag Bits with Bit Stuffing
docs.text:
• Allows frames to contain an arbitrary number of bits (bit-oriented framing). • Frame start and end are marked by the special flag bit pattern: 01111110 (six consecutive 1s). • Bit Stuffing Rule (Sender): • Whenever sender's data link layer encounters FIVE consecutive 1s in the payload, it automatically stuffs a 0 bit immediately after them into the outgoing bit stream. • Destuffing Rule (Receiver): • When receiver sees five consecutive 1s followed by a 0 bit, it automatically strips out the 0 bit. • If followed by a 1 bit and a 0 bit, it is a valid end-of-frame FLAG (01111110). • If followed by two 1 bits, an error has occurred (01111111). [Faculty — Slide 17-20 / General — Slide 20-22]

  Original Data:      01101111111001111101
  Stuffed Stream:     0110111110110011111001
                              ^         ^
                        (Stuffed 0s inserted)
──────

docs.title: Method 4: Physical Layer Coding Violations
docs.text: • Used in networks where Physical Layer encoding has inherent redundancy (e.g., Manchester encoding where every bit period has a signal transition). • High-High or Low-Low signals are invalid data transitions; they are used as delimiters to mark frame boundaries. [Faculty — Slide 21 / General — Slide 24] ──────

docs.title: 3.1 Error Types
docs.text: • Single-Bit Error: Only 1 bit of a data unit is inverted. • Burst Error: 2 or more bits in a data unit are corrupted. Length of burst k is measured from the first corrupted bit to the last corrupted bit. [Faculty — Slide 22] ──────

docs.title: 3.2 Error Control Strategies
docs.text: • Forward Error Correction (FEC): Sender includes enough redundant bits for receiver to detect AND correct errors without retransmission. Used on noisy/high-delay channels (wireless, satellite). [Faculty — Slide 22 / General — Slide 25] • Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ): Sender includes just enough redundancy to detect errors. Receiver requests retransmission upon detecting error. Used on low-noise channels (optical fiber). [Faculty — Slide 22 / General — Slide 25] ──────

docs.title: Definition: Hamming Distance
docs.text: The number of bit positions in which two binary codewords differ. Calculated by performing an XOR operation between two codewords and counting the number of 1s in the result. [Faculty — Slide 24 / General — Slide 26]

docs.title: Formula: Error Detection Requirement
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{min}} \ge d + 1 \]

To detect d single-bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance \(d_{\text{min}}\) of the code must be at least d + 1. [Faculty — Slide 25]

docs.title: Formula: Error Correction Requirement
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{min}} \ge 2p + 1 \]

To correct p single-bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance \(d_{\text{min}}\) must be at least 2p + 1. [Faculty — Slide 25]

docs.title: 3.4 The Hamming Code (Single-Bit Error Correcting Code)
Rules of Hamming Code Construction:
docs.text:
1. Bit positions are numbered starting at 1 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7...).
  2. Check bits (Parity bits \(P_k\)) are placed at positions that are powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…(\(2^k\)).
  3. Data bits (\(D_j\)) fill all remaining positions (3, 5, 6, 7, 9…). [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: Formula: Relationship Between Data Bits and Redundant Check Bits
docs.text:
For m data bits and r redundant check bits:

\[ (m + r + 1) \le 2^r \]

[Faculty — Slide 27]

docs.title: Step-by-Step Worked Numerical Example 1: Hamming Code Encoding
docs.text:
Problem: Encode the 4-bit data message \(D = 1101_2\) (\(D_4=1,D_3=1,D_2=0,D_1=1\)) into a (7,4) Hamming code using EVEN parity.

  • Given: Data \(m = 4\) bits (1101). \(r = 3\) check bits are required because:
\[ (m+r+1) \le 2^r \] \[ (4+3+1) \le 2^3 \] \[ 8 \le 8 \]

docs.title: Bit Positioning:
docs.text:
Bit Position:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7
Bit Type:     P1  P2  D1  P4  D2  D3  D4
Bit Value:    ?   ?   1   ?   0   1   1

docs.title: Parity Computation Groups:
docs.text:
• \(P_1\) checks positions (1,3,5,7):
\[ P_1,D_1,D_2,D_4 = P_1,1,0,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_1 = 0 \]
  • \(P_2\) checks positions (2,3,6,7):
\[ P_2,D_1,D_3,D_4 = P_2,1,1,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_2 = 1 \]
  • \(P_4\) checks positions (4,5,6,7):
\[ P_4,D_2,D_3,D_4 = P_4,0,1,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_4 = 0 \]

docs.title: Final Transmitted Codeword:
docs.text:
\[ \text{Codeword} = \mathbf{0110011} \]

[Faculty — Slide 29]

docs.title: 3.6 Internet Checksum (UDP Worked Numerical Example) [Faculty — Slide 33]
docs.text: • Data is treated as a sequence of 16-bit integers. • Integers are added together using 1's complement arithmetic. • The final sum is bitwise inverted (NOT operation).

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text: Mechanisms to prevent a fast transmitting node from swamping a slower receiving node with more data than its buffers can store. [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: 4.2 Three Flow Control Strategies
docs.text:
Flow Control Strategies
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
   Feedback-Based             Rate-Based               Credit-Based
 (Receiver sends ACKs)    (Built-in Rate Limit)   (Receiver grants credits)
  1. Feedback-Based Flow Control: Receiver sends feedback messages back to the sender giving explicit permission to transmit more data (e.g., Stop-and-Wait, Sliding Window ACKs). [Faculty — Slide 28 / General — Slide 28]
  2. Rate-Based Flow Control: Protocol mechanism limits transmission to a fixed data rate built-in, without explicit feedback frames. [Faculty — Slide 29 / General — Slide 29]
  3. Credit-Based Flow Control: Receiver grants sender explicit window credits (in bytes or frames). Sender deducts credits for each byte sent and stops when credits reach zero. [Faculty — Slide 30 / General — Slide 30] ──────

docs.title: 5.1 Protocol Environment Architecture
docs.text:
In Tanenbaum framework, protocol code interacts with lower (Physical) and upper (Network) layers via interface primitives:

• to_network_layer(p) / from_network_layer(&p) • to_physical_layer(&f) / from_physical_layer(&f) • start_timer(k) / stop_timer(k) • wait_for_event(&event) [Faculty — Slide 35-36 / General — Slide 34-36] ──────

docs.title: Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Communication is strictly unidirectional (Simplex).
  2. Physical channel is completely error-free.
  3. Receiver's network layer has infinite processing speed and buffer space (No flow control needed). [Faculty — Slide 37 / General — Slide 37]

docs.title: Mechanism:
docs.text:
Sender loops infinitely fetching packets from network layer and sending frames. Receiver loops infinitely waiting for frames and handing packets up.

// Sender (Utopian)
void sender1(void) {
    frame s; packet buffer;
    while (true) {
        from_network_layer(&buffer);
        s.info = buffer;
        to_physical_layer(&s);
    }
}
──────

docs.title: 5.3 Protocol 2: Simplex Stop-and-Wait Protocol for Error-Free Channel
Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Communication is unidirectional.
  2. Physical channel is error-free.
  3. Receiver has finite buffer capacity and limited processing speed. [Faculty — Slide 39 / General — Slide 39]

docs.title: Mechanism:
docs.text:
Sender sends 1 frame, then stops and waits until receiver sends back an explicit ACK dummy frame signaling it is ready for the next frame.

     Sender Machine                                Receiver Machine
  +------------------+                          +-------------------+
  | Send Frame 0     | -----------------------> | Receive Frame 0   |
  | (Wait for ACK)   |                          | Pass to Network L |
  |                  | <----------------------- | Send Dummy ACK    |
  | Receive ACK      |                          | (Wait for Frame)  |
  | Send Frame 1     | -----------------------> |                   |
  +------------------+                          +-------------------+
──────

docs.title: 5.4 Protocol 3: Simplex Stop-and-Wait for Noisy Channel (PAR)
Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Channel is noisy: frames can be corrupted or lost completely.
  2. ACKs can also be corrupted or lost. [Faculty — Slide 42 / General — Slide 42]

docs.title: Key Mechanisms added:
docs.text:
1. Timer & Retransmission: Sender sets a timer upon transmitting a frame. If ACK does not arrive before timer expires, sender retransmits.
  2. 1-Bit Sequence Numbers (0 and 1): Prevents duplicate frame acceptance when an ACK is delayed/lost. [Faculty — Slide 44 / General — Slide 44]

Normal Sequence: Sender --(Frame 0)--> Receiver --(ACK 0)--> Sender --(Frame 1)--> Receiver

Lost ACK Scenario: Sender --(Frame 0)--> Receiver (Gets Frame 0, Sends ACK 0 [LOST!]) Sender Timer Expires! Sender --(Retransmit Frame 0)--> Receiver (Sees Seq 0 duplicate, discards payload, re-sends ACK 0!) ──────

docs.title: 6.1 Bidirectional Transmission & Piggybacking
docs.text: • Piggybacking: Temporarily delaying an outgoing ACK so it can be hooked onto the header of the next outgoing data frame. • Timer for Piggybacking: If no outgoing data frame is generated within a short timeout, a separate ACK frame must be sent to avoid sender timeout. [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 48] ──────

docs.title: 6.2 Sequence Number Space & Window Concept
docs.text: • Sequence numbers range from 0 to MAX_SEQ = 2ⁿ - 1 (for n-bit sequence numbers). • Sender Window (Wₛ): Contains sequence numbers of frames sent but not yet acknowledged. • Receiver Window (Wᵣ): Contains sequence numbers of frames receiver is willing to accept. [Faculty — Slide 49 / General — Slide 49] ──────

docs.title: 6.3 Protocol 4: One-Bit Sliding Window (Wₛ = 1,Wᵣ = 1)
