docs.title: Detailed Operations of BIU & EU
docs.text:
1. Bus Interface Unit (BIU):
  2. Instruction Queue (Q): 6-byte First-In-First-Out (FIFO) buffer. The BIU prefetches up to 6 bytes of instruction code from memory whenever the queue has room for at least 2 bytes and the EU is not accessing memory.
  3. Segment Registers: CS, DS, SS, ES (16-bit registers storing base segment paragraph addresses).
  4. Instruction Pointer (IP): 16-bit register holding the offset address of the next instruction byte.

  5. Address Summing Block (\(\\\Sigma\)): Dedicated 20-bit adder that computes physical addresses from segment and offset registers.

  6. Execution Unit (EU):

  7. Control Unit: Fetches decoded instruction bytes from the output of the BIU queue and generates control signals for execution.
  8. 16-bit ALU: Executes arithmetic, logical, shift, and rotate operations.
  9. Register Set: Contains 8 general/pointer/index registers and 16-bit Flag register.
  10. Asynchronous Operation: BIU and EU operate independently. While EU executes an instruction, BIU prefetches subsequent instruction bytes, maximizing bus utilization (Pipelining).
  11. Queue Flushing: When EU encounters a branch/jump/call instruction, the pre-fetched queue bytes are flushed (cleared), and BIU fetches from the new branch target address.
flowchart TD
    subgraph BIU [Bus Interface Unit]
        fetch["Prefetch Instruction Bytes"] --> q["6-Byte FIFO Instruction Queue"]
    end
    subgraph EU [Execution Unit]
        q -->|Fetch Next Byte| decode["Decode Instruction"]
        decode --> exec["Execute Instruction"]
        exec --> branch{"Is Branch/Jump/Call?"}
        branch -->|Yes| flush["Flush / Clear Queue"]
        branch -->|No| cont["Continue Execution"]
    end
    flush -->|New Target Address| fetch

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 6, 7, 18–20]

docs.title: Comprehensive 8086 Register Array Specifications
docs.text:
Register Group Symbol Bit Size Split Registers Dedicated Functions Accumulator AX 16-bit AH (8-bit), AL (8-bit) Primary arithmetic/logic target, I/O port data transfers, fast multiplication/division. Base Register BX 16-bit BH (8-bit), BL (8-bit) Memory base address pointer for data references; indirect addressing. Count Register CX 16-bit CH (8-bit), CL (8-bit) Loop counter (LOOP), bit shift/rotate counter (CL), string operations. Data Register DX 16-bit DH (8-bit), DL (8-bit) 16-bit I/O port address pointer (IN/OUT); high-word holder in 32-bit math. Stack Pointer SP 16-bit None Offset address of Top-of-Stack within Stack Segment (SS). Base Pointer BP 16-bit None Base offset address for parameter passing inside stack frames (SS). Source Index SI 16-bit None Source data offset pointer in DS; source string pointer (DS:SI). Destination Index DI 16-bit None Destination data offset pointer in DS; string target pointer (ES:DI). Code Segment CS 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Code Segment. Data Segment DS 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Data Segment. Stack Segment SS 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Stack Segment. Extra Segment ES 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Extra Segment (string destinations). Instruction Pointer IP 16-bit None Offset address of next instruction to execute within CS (CS:IP).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 8–14, 19]

docs.title: 5. 8086 Flag Register Specifications
docs.text:
The 8086 Flag Register is a 16-bit register containing 9 active flags (6 Status Flags and 3 Control Flags):

Bit Position Flag Name Symbol Category Functional Description \(D_0\) Carry Flag CF Status Set to 1 if unsigned math produces carry out of MSB or borrow; otherwise 0. \(D_2\) Parity Flag PF Status Set to 1 if lower 8 bits of result contain even number of 1s (Even Parity). \(D_4\) Auxiliary Carry AF Status Set to 1 if carry generated from bit 3 to bit 4 during BCD math. \(D_6\) Zero Flag ZF Status Set to 1 if operation result is zero; reset to 0 if non-zero. \(D_7\) Sign Flag SF Status Set to 1 if MSB of result is 1 (negative signed value). \(D_8\) Trap Flag TF Control Set to 1 to enable single-step debugging mode (CPU generates Type 1 interrupt after each instruction). \(D_9\) Interrupt Flag IF Control Set to 1 to enable maskable hardware interrupts (INTR); 0 disables INTR. \(D_{10}\) Direction Flag DF Control Determines auto increment/decrement for string operations: 0 = Increment (forward), 1 = Decrement (backward). \(D_{11}\) Overflow Flag OF Status Set to 1 if signed arithmetic result exceeds signed capacity of destination register.

docs.title: Comprehensive Flag Calculation Example
docs.text:
Consider execution of ADD AL, 1 when register AL contains 7FH (\(0111\,1111_2\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Initial AL:} & \quad 0111\,1111_2 \quad (7\text{FH}) \\ + \text{Value } 1: & \quad 0000\,0001_2 \quad (01\text{H}) \\ \hline \text{New AL Result:} & \quad 1000\,0000_2 \quad (80\text{H}) \end{aligned} \]
  • AL Output: \(80\text{H}\) (Decimal \(-128\) in signed 2's complement).
  • Carry Flag (CF): 0 (No carry out of bit 7).
  • Parity Flag (PF): 0 (Result \(1000\,0000_2\) has one 1 bit \(\rightarrow\) odd parity).
  • Auxiliary Carry (AF): 1 (Carry generated out of bit 3 into bit 4).
  • Zero Flag (ZF): 0 (Result \(80\text{H}\) is non-zero).
  • Sign Flag (SF): 1 (Bit \(D_7\) is 1).
  • Overflow Flag (OF): 1 (Positive \(+127\) added to \(+1\) resulted in negative \(-128\), triggering signed overflow).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 15–17]

docs.title: Concept of Segmented Memory
docs.text:
The 8086 addresses \(1\text{ MB}\) (\(1,048,576\text{ bytes}\)) of physical memory using a 20-bit address. However, all internal registers are 16-bit wide. To bridge this gap, memory is organized into logical Segments.

  • A Segment is a contiguous block of up to \(64\text{ KB}\) (\(65,536\text{ bytes}\)) of memory.
  • A segment can begin at any memory address divisible by 16 (\(10\text{H}\)), known as a Paragraph Boundary (where the lower 4 hex digits of physical address are 0000_2).
  • Four active logical segments are accessible at any instant: Code Segment (CS), Data Segment (DS), Stack Segment (SS), and Extra Segment (ES).

docs.title: Key Architectural Advantages of Memory Segmentation
docs.text:
1. Expands Memory Capacity: Allows 16-bit registers to address \(1\text{ MB}\) of physical memory using segment:offset combinations.
  2. Code and Data Protection: Separates executable code, data variables, and stack buffers into distinct logical areas, preventing accidental program overwrite.
  3. Dynamic Program Relocation: Programs can be loaded into any physical memory location without altering internal offset addresses—only the segment register values are updated.
  4. Supports Programs \(>\) 64 KB: Code, data, or stack structures exceeding \(64\text{ KB}\) can be handled by defining multiple logical segments.

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 21–24]

docs.title: Memory Banking (Physical Organization)
docs.text:
Although the 8086 has a 20-bit address bus to access 1 MB of physical memory, the memory is physically organized as two independent 512 KB banks: the Even Bank (Low Bank) and the Odd Bank (High Bank). This allows the 16-bit CPU to access either an 8-bit byte or a 16-bit word in a single bus cycle.

  • Even Bank (Low Bank): Contains all even-numbered physical addresses (00000H, 00002H, ... FFFFEH). Connected to the lower half of the data bus (\(D_7 - D_0\)). It is enabled when address line \(A_0 = 0\).
  • Odd Bank (High Bank): Contains all odd-numbered physical addresses (00001H, 00003H, ... FFFFFH). Connected to the upper half of the data bus (\(D_{15} - D_8\)). It is enabled when Bus High Enable (\(\overline{\text{BHE}}\)) pin is active low (\(\overline{\text{BHE}} = 0\)).
flowchart TD
    subgraph Mem["8086 1 MB Physical Memory Space"]
        subgraph Even["Even Bank / Low Bank<br>Enables D7-D0<br>Activated when A0 = 0"]
            even_mem["512 KB Even Addresses<br>00000H, 00002H, ... FFFFEH"]
        end
        subgraph Odd["Odd Bank / High Bank<br>Enables D15-D8<br>Activated when BHE = 0"]
            odd_mem["512 KB Odd Addresses<br>00001H, 00003H, ... FFFFFH"]
        end
    end
    8086["8086 CPU"] -->|BHE Signal| Odd
    8086 -->|A0 Signal| Even

docs.title: Bank Selection and Alignment Scenarios (Exam Twisters)
docs.text:
The 8086 uses \(A_0\) and \(\overline{\text{BHE}}\) status signals to select the appropriate memory bank(s) according to this truth table:

\(\overline{\text{BHE}}\) \(A_0\) Data Bus Width Used Memory Bank Accessed Bus Cycles Required 0 0 16-bit (\(D_{15} - D_0\)) Both Banks (Aligned Word access at Even Address) 1 Cycle 0 1 8-bit (\(D_{15} - D_8\)) Odd Bank only (Byte access at Odd Address) 1 Cycle 1 0 8-bit (\(D_7 - D_0\)) Even Bank only (Byte access at Even Address) 1 Cycle 1 1 None (Idle) No Bank selected -

CRITICAL EXAM TWISTER (Unaligned Word Access): If the CPU attempts to read/write a 16-bit word starting at an odd address (e.g., 00001H), it is called an unaligned word access. This requires two consecutive bus cycles: 1. First Bus Cycle: CPU accesses the Odd Bank (\(\overline{\text{BHE}}=0, A_0=1\)) to read the low byte of the word from 00001H using \(D_{15}-D_8\). 2. Second Bus Cycle: CPU accesses the Even Bank (\(\overline{\text{BHE}}=1, A_0=0\)) to read the high byte of the word from 00002H using \(D_7-D_0\).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slide 25]

docs.title: Figure 3.3: 8086 Physical Address Summing Block
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Seg["Segment Register<br>e.g., CS = 3000H"] -->|Shift Left 4 Bits<br>Multiply by 10H| Shift["Base Segment Address<br>30000H"]
    Offset["Offset Register<br>e.g., IP = 1234H"] --> Add
    Shift --> Add((20-Bit Adder))
    Add -->|Sum| PA["Physical Address<br>31234H"]

docs.title: Mathematical Formula
docs.text:
\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 16_{10}) + \text{Offset Address} \]

In Hexadecimal notation:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 10_H) + \text{Offset Address} \] 
Segment Register (16-bit):  [ S3  S2  S1  S0 ] 0H    (Shifted 4 bits left = x 16)
+ Offset Register (16-bit):      [ O3  O2  O1  O0 ]
---------------------------------------------------
Physical Address (20-bit):  [ P4  P3  P2  P1  P0 ]

CRITICAL EXAM TWISTER (Physical Address Wrap-around in Real Mode): What happens if the segment and offset combination computes an address exceeding the 1 MB addressable boundary (FFFFFH)? For example: \(\text{Segment} = \text{FFFFH}\), \(\text{Offset} = \text{FFFFH}\).

\[ \text{Base Segment Address} = \text{FFFFH} \times 10\text{H} = \text{FFFF0H} \] \[ \text{Physical Address} = \text{FFFF0H} + \text{FFFFH} = \text{10FFEFH} \]

Since the 8086 has only 20 physical address lines (\(A_{19} - A_0\)), the 21st bit (the leading 1 in 10FFEFH) is discarded (there is no 21st line). The address wraps around to the very beginning of physical memory space, specifically to:

\[ \text{Wrapped Address} = \text{0FFEFH} \]

This is a classic real-mode memory limitation and an extremely common trick question in university examinations.

docs.title: Standard Segment and Offset Register Pairs
docs.text:
Segment Type Segment Register Default Offset Register Alternative Offset Registers Physical Address Purpose Instruction Fetch CS IP None Next instruction byte to fetch (CS:IP). Stack Operation SS SP BP Top of stack (SS:SP) or stack frame (SS:BP). General Data DS BX SI, DI, Direct Address General variable data (DS:BX, DS:SI, DS:DI). String Destination ES DI None Destination operand in string commands (ES:DI).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 26, 32]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3.1
docs.text: Problem: The Data Segment (DS) starts at physical address 10000H (Segment value 1000H). A data reference specifies an offset of 0029H. Calculate the physical address of the data operand. Given: \(\text{DS} = 1000\text{H}\), \(\text{Offset} = 0029\text{H}\). Required: Physical Address. Formula: \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{DS} \times 10\text{H} + \text{Offset}\). Solution Steps: 1. Shift DS value left by 4 hex bits: \(1000\text{H} \times 10\text{H} = 10000\text{H}\). 2. Add offset: \(10000\text{H} + 0029\text{H} = 10029\text{H}\). Final Answer: Physical Address = 10029H.

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3.2
docs.text:
Problem: A program code segment starts at physical address 70400H. 1. What value is stored in the Code Segment register (CS)? 2. If the Instruction Pointer (IP) contains 539CH, what physical address is fetched?

Given: \(\text{Physical Base} = 70400\text{H}\), \(\text{IP} = 539\text{CH}\). Required: CS register value, physical fetch address. Formula: \(\text{CS} = \frac{\text{Physical Base}}{16_{10}}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{CS} \times 10\text{H} + \text{IP}\). Solution Steps: 1. \(\text{CS} = \frac{70400\text{H}}{10\text{H}} = 7040\text{H}\). 2. \(\text{Physical Address} = 70400\text{H} + 539\text{CH} = 7579\text{CH}\). Final Answer: CS = 7040H, Physical Address = 7579CH.

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3.3
docs.text:
Problem: The Stack Segment register (SS) contains 3000H and Stack Pointer (SP) contains 8434H. Find the physical address of the top of stack. Given: \(\text{SS} = 3000\text{H}\), \(\text{SP} = 8434\text{H}\). Required: Physical Address of Top of Stack. Formula: \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{SS} \times 10\text{H} + \text{SP}\). Solution Steps:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = 30000\text{H} + 8434\text{H} = 38434\text{H} \]

Final Answer: Top of Stack Physical Address = 38434H.

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 31, 33]

docs.title: Key 8086 Pin Signals
docs.text:
1. \(AD_{15} - AD_0\) (Pins 1–16, 39): Multiplexed Address/Data bus. Carries memory address during \(T_1\), and data during \(T_2, T_3, T_4\).
  2. \(A_{19}/S_6 - A_{16}/S_3\) (Pins 35–38): Multiplexed high address lines and system status lines.
  3. \(\overline{\text{BHE}}/S_7\) (Pin 34): Bus High Enable / Status. Active low signal used to enable upper data byte (\(D_{15} - D_8\)) on memory bus.
  4. \(\text{MN}/\overline{\text{MX}}\) (Pin 33): Minimum / Maximum mode select. High selects Minimum mode; Low selects Maximum mode.
  5. \(RD\) (Pin 32): Read signal. Active low.
  6. \(TEST\) (Pin 23): Tested by WAIT instruction. If low, CPU continues execution; if high, CPU waits.
  7. \(READY\) (Pin 22): Bus ready input for interfacing slow memories.
  8. \(RESET\) (Pin 21): Reset input. Clears flags, IP to 0000H, CS to FFFFH.

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slide 4]

docs.title: 9. 8086 Addressing Modes
docs.text: The 8086 provides 7 primary addressing modes for accessing instruction operands:

docs.title: Summary Comparison Table of Addressing Modes
docs.text: Addressing Mode Effective Address (\(EA\)) Formula Advantage Disadvantage Typical Assembly Example Register \(EA = R\) Fastest (No memory reference) Limited addressable space (registers only) MOV BX, DX Immediate \(EA = \text{Instruction Constant}\) Fast operand loading Fixed constant value MOV AX, 2550H Direct \(EA = [\text{Displacement}]\) Simple to program Fixed memory offset MOV AX, [2400H] Register Indirect \(EA = [\text{BX/BP/SI/DI}]\) Large addressable memory Requires prior register load MOV AX, [BX] Base Relative \(EA = [\text{BX/BP}] + \text{Disp}\) Flexible for structures Requires 16-bit register addition MOV AX, 12H[BX] Indexed Relative \(EA = [\text{SI/DI}] + \text{Disp}\) Ideal for array indexing Requires 16-bit register addition MOV DX, ARRAY[SI] Base Indexed Relative \(EA = [\text{BX/BP}] + [\text{SI/DI}] + \text{Disp}\) Extremely flexible (2D arrays) Complex address calculation MOV AX, BETA[BX][SI]

docs.title: Detailed Breakdown of Each Addressing Mode
1. Register Addressing Mode
docs.text: Operand is stored inside an internal CPU register.

docs.title: Figure 3.5: Register Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = R\)
  • Example: MOV BX, DX (Copies contents of DX into BX).

docs.title: 2. Immediate Addressing Mode
docs.text: Operand data is encoded directly as part of the machine instruction byte sequence.

docs.title: Figure 3.6: Immediate Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(\text{Operand} = A\)
  • Example: MOV AX, 2550H (Loads immediate word 2550H into AX).

    CRITICAL EXAM WARNING (Segment Register Load Restriction): Inside the 8086 Instruction Set Architecture, immediate data cannot be loaded directly into any Segment Register (CS, DS, SS, ES). - Invalid/Illegal: MOV DS, 1000H (Will result in a compiler/assembler error). - Correct Workaround: You must load the immediate value into a 16-bit general purpose register (like AX, BX, CX, DX) first, and then copy that register into the target Segment Register: 

    MOV AX, 1000H   ; Load immediate data into AX
MOV DS, AX      ; Transfer from AX to DS

docs.title: 3. Direct Addressing Mode
docs.text: The 16-bit effective address (offset) of the operand is explicitly written inside the instruction.

docs.title: Figure 3.7: Direct Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = A\), \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{DS} \times 10\text{H} + A\)
  • Example: MOV AX, [2400H] (If \(\text{DS} = 2000\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 20000\text{H} + 2400\text{H} = 22400\text{H}\)).

docs.title: 4. Register Indirect Addressing Mode
docs.text: The 16-bit offset address of the operand in memory is held inside a Base register (BX, BP) or Index register (SI, DI).

docs.title: Figure 3.8: Register Indirect Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [R]\) where \(R \in \{\text{BX}, \text{BP}, \text{SI}, \text{DI}\}\)
  • Example: MOV AX, [BX] (If \(\text{DS} = 1010\text{H}\) and \(\text{BX} = 1122\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 10100\text{H} + 1122\text{H} = 11222\text{H}\)).
  • Pointer Operator Requirement: In ambiguous memory operations, BYTE PTR or WORD PTR must specify data size (e.g., INC BYTE PTR [BX]).

docs.title: 5. Base Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text: Effective address is computed by adding an 8-bit or 16-bit displacement to the contents of a Base register (BX or BP).

docs.title: Figure 3.9: Base Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)
  • Default Segment for BX is DS.
  • Default Segment for BP is SS.
  • Displacement Limits: 8-bit signed (\(-128\) to \(+127\)) or 16-bit signed (\(-32768\) to \(+32767\)).
  • Example: MOV AX, 1234H[BX] (If \(\text{DS} = 4000\text{H}\), \(\text{BX} = 1000\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 40000\text{H} + 1000\text{H} + 1234\text{H} = 42234\text{H}\)).

docs.title: 6. Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text: Effective address is computed by adding an 8-bit or 16-bit displacement to an Index register (SI or DI).

docs.title: Figure 3.10: Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)
  • Example: MOV DX, ARRAY[SI] (If \(\text{DS} = 2000\text{H}\), \(\text{SI} = 5000\text{H}\), \(\text{ARRAY} = 1234\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 20000\text{H} + 5000\text{H} + 1234\text{H} = 26234\text{H}\)).

docs.title: 7. Base Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text: Combines Base register, Index register, and an optional displacement to compute the effective address.

docs.title: Figure 3.11: Base Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)
  • Example: MOV AX, BETA[BX][SI] (If \(\text{DS} = 1200\text{H}\), \(\text{BX} = 1000\text{H}\), \(\text{SI} = 2000\text{H}\), \(\text{BETA} = 1234\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 12000\text{H} + 1000\text{H} + 2000\text{H} + 1234\text{H} = 15234\text{H}\)).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture, Slides 34–54]

docs.title: 10. 8086 Instruction Format & Machine Encoding
docs.text: 8086 instructions range from 1 to 6 bytes in length.

docs.title: Field Descriptions in Machine Code Byte
docs.text:
1. Opcode (6 bits): Identifies basic instruction operation (e.g., 100010_2 for MOV).
  2. D (Direction Bit, 1 bit):
  3. \(D = 0\): Data flows from Register specified in REG field to operand in R/M.
  4. \(D = 1\): Data flows to Register specified in REG field from operand in R/M.
  5. W (Word/Byte Bit, 1 bit):
  6. \(W = 0\): 8-bit Byte operation.
  7. \(W = 1\): 16-bit Word operation.
  8. MOD (Mode Field, 2 bits): Specifies addressing mode (Register vs Memory with displacement):
  9. \(\text{MOD} = 11\): Register-to-Register mode (No memory displacement).
  10. \(\text{MOD} = 00\): Memory mode with no displacement (except direct addressing when \(\text{R/M} = 110\)).
  11. \(\text{MOD} = 01\): Memory mode with 8-bit sign-extended displacement.
  12. \(\text{MOD} = 10\): Memory mode with 16-bit displacement.
  13. REG (Register Field, 3 bits): Identifies register operand.
  14. R/M (Register/Memory Field, 3 bits): Specifies second operand or memory addressing combination.

docs.title: Figure 3.13: 8086 MOD and R/M Encoding Matrix
docs.text: [Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture, Slides 55–66]

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text: This chapter provides an exhaustive breakdown of the 8086 microprocessor instruction set. Instructions are classified into functional categories: Data Transfer, Arithmetic, Logical, Shift/Rotate, String Manipulation, Branch/Control Transfer, and Processor Control. Each instruction is detailed with syntax, operational mechanics, flag impacts, constraints, worked code examples, and practical programming patterns.

docs.title: 2. General Assembler Instruction Syntax
docs.text:
The standard format for an 8086 assembly language instruction line is:

Label:   Mnemonic   Destination, Source   ; Comments

docs.title: Example
docs.text: START:   MOV        AX, [BX]              ; Load word from memory address BX into AX

docs.title: Pointer (PTR) Operator Resolution
docs.text:
When an instruction contains a memory operand without an explicit register to specify operand size, the assembler cannot determine whether to execute a 8-bit byte or 16-bit word operation. The PTR operator must be used to resolve ambiguity:

  • INC [BX] \(\rightarrow\) AMBIGUOUS (Compiler Error).
  • INC BYTE PTR [BX] \(\rightarrow\) Increments the 8-bit byte at memory address [BX].
  • INC WORD PTR [BX] \(\rightarrow\) Increments the 16-bit word at memory address [BX].

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 3, 5]

docs.title: 3. Data Transfer Instructions
docs.text: Data transfer instructions move data between registers, memory locations, and I/O ports. No status flags are affected by standard data transfer instructions.

docs.title: MOV (Move Data)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Copies data byte or word from source to destination.
  • Syntax: MOV Destination, Source
  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Source})\)
  • Constraints:
  • Both operands cannot be memory locations simultaneously.
  • Both operands cannot be segment registers simultaneously.
  • Immediate data cannot be moved directly into segment registers.
  • Flags Affected: None.
  • Examples: 
    MOV CX, 037AH        ; Load immediate word 037AH into CX
MOV AL, BL           ; Copy byte from BL to AL
MOV BX, [0301H]      ; Load word from memory offset 0301H into BX

docs.title: XCHG (Exchange Data)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Swaps contents of source and destination operands.
  • Syntax: XCHG Destination, Source
  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftrightarrow (\text{Source})\)
  • Constraints: Cannot exchange two memory locations directly. One operand must be a register. Segment registers cannot be exchanged.
  • Flags Affected: None.
  • Examples: 
    XCHG BX, AX          ; Swap contents of BX and AX
XCHG [5000H], AX     ; Swap word in memory location 5000H with AX

docs.title: LEA (Load Effective Address)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Computes the 16-bit effective address (offset) of the source memory operand and stores it in the destination register.
  • Syntax: LEA Reg16, Memory
  • Operation: \(\text{EA} \rightarrow (\text{Reg16})\)
  • Flags Affected: None.
  • Example: 
    LEA BX, ARRAY        ; Load offset address of ARRAY into register BX

docs.title: LDS (Load Pointer Using DS)
docs.text: • Purpose: Loads a 32-bit far pointer from a 4-byte memory location into a 16-bit general register and the Data Segment register (DS).

docs.title: Figure 4.1: LDS and LES Memory Pointer Loading Mechanism
docs.text:
• Syntax: LDS Reg16, MEM32
  • Operation:
  • \((\text{MEM32}) \rightarrow (\text{Reg16})\) (Offset loaded into destination register)
  • \((\text{MEM32} + 2) \rightarrow (\text{DS})\) (Segment selector loaded into DS)
  • Flags Affected: None.
  • Example: 
    LDS SI, [0301H]      ; Loads offset into SI and segment into DS from memory 0301H

docs.title: LES (Load Pointer Using ES)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Loads a 32-bit far pointer from memory into a specified 16-bit register and the Extra Segment register (ES).
  • Syntax: LES Reg16, MEM32
  • Operation:
  • \((\text{MEM32}) \rightarrow (\text{Reg16})\)
  • \((\text{MEM32} + 2) \rightarrow (\text{ES})\)
  • Flags Affected: None.
  • Example: 
    LES BX, STRING_PTR   ; Loads string offset into BX and segment into ES

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 7–14]

docs.title: 4. Arithmetic Instructions
docs.text: Arithmetic instructions perform binary addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, increment, decrement, and sign extension. All conditional flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF) are affected unless explicitly noted.

docs.title: ADD (Add Words or Bytes)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Adds contents of source operand to destination operand and stores sum in destination.
  • Syntax: ADD Destination, Source
  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) + (\text{Source})\)
  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).
  • Examples: 
    ADD AX, 2020H        ; AX = AX + 2020H
ADD AX, BX           ; AX = AX + BX

docs.title: ADC (Add with Carry)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Adds source operand, destination operand, and the current Carry Flag (CF) bit together.
  • Syntax: ADC Destination, Source
  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) + (\text{Source}) + \text{CF}\)
  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).
  • Examples: 
    ADC AX, 2020H        ; AX = AX + 2020H + CF
ADC AX, BX           ; AX = AX + BX + CF

docs.title: SUB (Subtract)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Subtracts source operand from destination operand.
  • Syntax: SUB Destination, Source
  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) - (\text{Source})\)
  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).
  • Examples: 
    SUB AX, 1000H        ; AX = AX - 1000H
SUB AX, BX           ; AX = AX - BX

docs.title: SBB (Subtract with Borrow)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Subtracts source operand and Carry Flag (Borrow) from destination operand.
  • Syntax: SBB Destination, Source
  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) - (\text{Source}) - \text{CF}\)
  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).
  • Examples: 
    SBB AX, 1000H        ; AX = AX - 1000H - CF
SBB AX, BX           ; AX = AX - BX - CF

docs.title: INC (Increment) & DEC (Decrement)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Adds 1 to (INC) or subtracts 1 from (DEC) the operand.
  • Syntax: INC Source, DEC Source
  • CRITICAL FLAG RULE: INC and DEC affect PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF, but DO NOT affect the Carry Flag (CF)!
  • Constraints: Operand cannot be immediate data.
  • Examples: 
    INC AX               ; Increment AX by 1
DEC BYTE PTR [5000H] ; Decrement byte in memory location 5000H by 1

CRITICAL EXAM TWISTER (Why INC/DEC do not affect CF): If you have a loop that performs multi-word additions using ADC (Add with Carry), you typically use a register like SI or DI to point to the array elements, and a loop register like CX or BX as a counter. After each array addition, you increment the pointer using INC SI and decrement the counter using DEC CX. If INC or DEC affected the Carry Flag, they would overwrite the carry status generated by the ADC instruction. This would ruin the addition of the next word/byte in the sequence! By leaving CF untouched, the 8086 allows developers to update pointers and counters inside multi-word arithmetic loops without losing valuable carry information.

docs.title: NEG (Negate / Two's Complement)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Replaces operand contents with its two's complement (\(0 - \text{Operand}\)).
  • Syntax: NEG Source
  • Flags Affected: All status flags. CF is set to 1 for any non-zero operand.
  • Example: 
    NEG AX               ; AX = -AX

docs.title: CMP (Compare)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Subtracts source operand from destination operand to update status flags without altering destination contents.
  • Syntax: CMP Operand1, Operand2
  • Operation: Flags updated based on \((\text{Operand1}) - (\text{Operand2})\). Result is discarded.
  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).
  • Examples: 
    CMP AX, 1000H        ; Compare AX with 1000H
CMP AX, BX           ; Compare AX with BX

docs.title: CBW (Convert Byte to Word) & CWD (Convert Word to Doubleword)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Sign-extends signed operands for division/arithmetic.
  • CBW: Extends sign bit of AL (\(D_7\)) across all bits of AH.
  • CWD: Extends sign bit of AX (\(D_{15}\)) across all bits of DX.
  • Syntax: CBW, CWD (No explicit operands).
  • Flags Affected: None.
  • Example Code Sequence (Adding Signed Byte Y to Signed Word X): 
    MOV AL, Y            ; Load signed byte Y into AL
CBW                  ; Sign extend AL into AX (AX now holds 16-bit signed Y)
ADD AX, X            ; Add signed word X to AX

docs.title: MUL (Unsigned Multiplication) & IMUL (Signed Multiplication)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Multiplies accumulator by source operand.
  • Operational Mechanics:
  • 8-bit Multiplication: \(\text{AL} \times \text{Operand8} \rightarrow \text{AX}\) (16-bit product stored in AX).
  • 16-bit Multiplication: \(\text{AX} \times \text{Operand16} \rightarrow (\text{DX:AX})\) (32-bit product stored across DX:AX, where DX holds high word).
  • Flags Affected: OF and CF are set to 1 if upper half of product contains significant digits (non-zero for MUL, non-sign extension for IMUL); otherwise reset to 0. Other flags are undefined.
  • Constraints: Source operand cannot be immediate data.
  • Examples: 
    MUL BH               ; AX = AL * BH (Unsigned)
IMUL CX              ; (DX:AX) = AX * CX (Signed)

docs.title: DIV (Unsigned Division) & IDIV (Signed Division)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Divides accumulator by source operand.
  • Operational Mechanics:
  • 8-bit Division: Dividend in AX \(\div\) Operand8 \(\rightarrow \text{AL} = \text{Quotient}\), \(\text{AH} = \text{Remainder}\).
  • 16-bit Division: Dividend in (DX:AX) \(\div\) Operand16 \(\rightarrow \text{AX} = \text{Quotient}\), \(\text{DX} = \text{Remainder}\).
  • Flags Affected: All status flags are undefined.
  • Examples: 
    MOV AX, 0203H
MOV BL, 04H
DIV BL               ; AX / BL -> AL = 50H (Quotient), AH = 03H (Remainder)

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 15–32]

docs.title: 5. Logical Instructions
docs.text:
Logical instructions perform bitwise boolean operations. CF and OF are cleared to 0 by all bitwise logical operations; SF, ZF, and PF are updated accordingly; AF is undefined.

Instruction Syntax Boolean Operation Flag Rules NOT NOT OPR \((\text{OPR}) \leftarrow \overline{\text{OPR}}\) (One's Complement) No flags affected. AND AND DST, SRC \((\text{DST}) \leftarrow (\text{DST}) \land (\text{SRC})\) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF. OR OR DST, SRC \((\text{DST}) \leftarrow (\text{DST}) \lor (\text{SRC})\) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF. XOR XOR DST, SRC \((\text{DST}) \leftarrow (\text{DST}) \oplus (\text{SRC})\) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF. TEST TEST OPR1, OPR2 \((\text{OPR1}) \land (\text{OPR2})\) (Result discarded) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF.

docs.title: Applied Bitwise Logic Program Example
docs.text:
Task: Selectively set bits 0 and 2 of DL; toggle (invert) bits 1 and 6; clear bits 3 and 4; then test bits 1 and 7 and branch to EXIT if both test bits are set.

OR  DL, 00000101B      ; Set bits 0 and 2 of DL (Mask: 05H)
XOR DL, 01000010B      ; Toggle bits 1 and 6 of DL (Mask: 42H)
AND DL, 11100111B      ; Clear bits 3 and 4 of DL (Mask: E7H)
TEST DL, 10000010B     ; Test bits 1 and 7 of DL (Mask: 82H)
JZ  EXIT               ; Jump to EXIT if tested bits are zero

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 33–34]

docs.title: 6. Shift and Rotate Instructions
docs.text:
Shift and Rotate instructions manipulate operand bits by shifting them left or right.

  • Count Rule: The shift/rotate count CNT can be 1 (specified as immediate constant) or stored in register CL for multi-bit shifts.
Instruction Name / Type Operational Behavior Carry Flag (CF) Impact SHL / SAL Shift Logical/Arithmetic Left Shifts bits left; fills right with 0. MSB shifted out enters CF. SHR Shift Logical Right Shifts bits right; fills left with 0. LSB shifted out enters CF. SAR Shift Arithmetic Right Shifts bits right; retains original MSB (sign bit) on left. LSB shifted out enters CF. ROL Rotate Left Circular bit rotation left. MSB rotates into LSB AND into CF. ROR Rotate Right Circular bit rotation right. LSB rotates into MSB AND into CF. RCL Rotate Left Through Carry 9-bit/17-bit circular rotation left through CF. CF bit enters LSB; MSB enters CF. RCR Rotate Right Through Carry 9-bit/17-bit circular rotation right through CF. CF bit enters MSB; LSB enters CF.

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 35–36]

docs.title: 7. Branch & Control Transfer Instructions
docs.text: Branch instructions alter program execution flow by modifying IP (and CS for Far branches).

docs.title: Unconditional Jump
docs.text: • JMP Target: Unconditionally branches to Target address.

docs.title: Conditional Jumps (Depend on Flag States)
docs.text:
• JZ / JE Target: Jump if Zero (\(ZF = 1\)).
  • JNZ / JNE Target: Jump if Not Zero (\(ZF = 0\)).
  • JC / JB Target: Jump if Carry / Below (\(CF = 1\)).
  • JNC / JNB Target: Jump if No Carry / Above or Equal (\(CF = 0\)).
  • JS Target: Jump if Sign / Negative (\(SF = 1\)).
  • JNS Target: Jump if No Sign / Positive (\(SF = 0\)).
  • JO Target: Jump if Overflow (\(OF = 1\)).
  • JPO / JNP Target: Jump if Parity Odd (\(PF = 0\)).
  • JPE / JP Target: Jump if Parity Even (\(PF = 1\)).

docs.title: Loop Control Instructions
docs.text:
• LOOP Target: Decrements CX by 1; jumps to Target if \( ext{CX} eq 0\).
  • LOOPE / LOOPZ Target: Decrements CX; jumps if \( ext{CX} eq 0\) AND \(ZF = 1\).
  • LOOPNE / LOOPNZ Target: Decrements CX; jumps if \( ext{CX} eq 0\) AND \(ZF = 0\).

docs.title: Subroutine Control
docs.text:
• CALL ProcedureName: Pushes return address (IP) onto stack and branches to procedure.
  • RET: Pops return address off stack into IP to return from procedure.

docs.title: 8. Processor Control & Flag Manipulation Instructions
docs.text:
• CLC: Clear Carry Flag (\(CF \leftarrow 0\)).
  • STC: Set Carry Flag (\(CF \leftarrow 1\)).
  • CMC: Complement Carry Flag (\(CF \leftarrow \overline{CF}\)).
  • CLD: Clear Direction Flag (\(DF \leftarrow 0\), Auto-increment string pointers).
  • STD: Set Direction Flag (\(DF \leftarrow 1\), Auto-decrement string pointers).
  • CLI: Clear Interrupt Flag (\(IF \leftarrow 0\), Disable maskable INTR).
  • STI: Set Interrupt Flag (\(IF \leftarrow 1\), Enable maskable INTR).
  • NOP: No Operation (Consumes 3 T-states, performs no operation).
  • HLT: Halt CPU execution until hardware interrupt or reset occurs.

docs.title: 1. 8085 Clock Period & T-State Duration
docs.text:
\[ T = \frac{1}{f_{\text{CLK}}} \]

Where \(f_{\text{CLK}}\) is CPU operating frequency (e.g., \(3\text{ MHz} \rightarrow T = 333.33\text{ ns}\)).

docs.title: 2. 8085 Hardware Interrupt Vector Address
docs.text:
\[ \text{Vector Address (Hex)} = (N \times 8_{10}) \quad \text{converted to 16-bit Hex} \]

Where \(N\) is restart vector number (e.g., \(RST 7.5 \rightarrow 7.5 \times 8 = 60_{10} = 003C_H\)).

docs.title: 3. Physical Address Calculation
docs.text:
\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 16_{10}) + \text{Offset Address} \] \[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 10_H) + \text{Offset Address} \]

Where: * \(\text{Segment Register} \in \{\text{CS}, \text{DS}, \text{SS}, \text{ES}\}\) (16-bit Base Selector). * \(\text{Offset Address} \in \{\text{IP}, \text{SP}, \text{BP}, \text{BX}, \text{SI}, \text{DI}, \text{Direct Address}\}\) (16-bit Offset).

docs.title: 4. Effective Address (\(EA\)) Formulas
docs.text:
• Register: \(EA = R\)
  • Immediate: \(\text{Operand} = A\)
  • Direct: \(EA = A\)
  • Register Indirect: \(EA = [R] \quad (R \in \{\text{BX}, \text{BP}, \text{SI}, \text{DI}\})\)
  • Base Relative: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + \text{Displacement} \quad (\text{Base} \in \{\text{BX}, \text{BP}\})\)
  • Indexed Relative: \(EA = [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement} \quad (\text{Index} \in \{\text{SI}, \text{DI}\})\)
  • Base Indexed Relative: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)

docs.title: Appendix B — Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Accumulator: Primary register used to store inputs and output results of ALU operations.
  • Address Bus: Unidirectional bus lines used by CPU to select memory or I/O locations.
  • Address Latch Enable (ALE): Signal issued to demultiplex address/data bus during \(T_1\).
  • Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): Digital circuit performing binary math and logic operations.
  • Bus Interface Unit (BIU): 8086 section responsible for fetching instructions, bus access, and address translation.
  • Execution Unit (EU): 8086 section responsible for instruction decoding and execution.
  • Instruction Queue: FIFO buffer in 8086 BIU holding prefetched instruction bytes.
  • Machine Cycle: Fundamental CPU bus operation (Fetch, Read, Write) composed of T-states.
  • Paragraph Boundary: Physical memory address divisible by 16 (ending in lower hex 0).
  • Pipelining: Overlapping instruction fetch and execution cycles to increase CPU throughput.
  • Segment Register: 16-bit register holding upper 16 bits of a 64 KB memory segment base address.
  • T-State: Single clock period of CPU system clock.
  • Vector Address: Fixed memory location to which CPU transfers execution upon receiving an interrupt.

docs.title: Appendix E — Exam Review & Questions
docs.text: This section provides an Exam-oriented review and question bank to test core microprocessor concepts.

docs.title: Section 1: Conceptual & Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the purpose of the ALE signal in Intel 8085 and 8086 microprocessors. Answer: \(ALE\) (Address Latch Enable) is a positive pulse emitted during \(T_1\) of a machine cycle to signal external latches (e.g., 74LS373) to capture and hold the lower address byte from the multiplexed Address/Data bus (\(AD_7 - AD_0\) or \(AD_{15} - AD_0\)).

  2. Why does the INC instruction in 8086 not affect the Carry Flag (CF)? Answer: INC (and DEC) instructions intentionally leave CF unaffected so that loop counter increments do not overwrite the carry state resulting from prior multi-word arithmetic operations.

  3. What is the difference between MUL and IMUL instructions in 8086? Answer: MUL performs unsigned binary multiplication, interpreting operands as positive magnitudes. IMUL performs signed two's complement multiplication, preserving operand sign bits.

  4. State two primary advantages of memory segmentation in the 8086 microprocessor. Answer: 1) Allows 16-bit registers to address \(1\text{ MB}\) of physical memory. 2) Enables dynamic code and data relocation without modifying internal program offset addresses.

docs.title: Section 2: Architectural & Diagram-Based Questions
docs.text:
1. Draw and explain the internal architecture of 8086, highlighting BIU and EU interaction. Review Requirement: Draw Figure 3.1. Explain prefetch queue operations, asynchronous execution, address generation, and queue flushing during branches.

  2. Explain the 8085 Interrupt structure in order of priority. Review Requirement: List priority: TRAP \(>\) RST 7.5 \(>\) RST 6.5 \(>\) RST 5.5 \(>\) INTR. Detail vector addresses, triggering mechanisms (edge vs level), and masking via SIM.

docs.title: Section 3: Numerical & Address Calculation Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. If \(\text{CS} = 24A0\text{H}\) and \(\text{IP} = 1082\text{H}\), determine the physical memory address. Solution:
\[ \text{Physical Address} = 24A00\text{H} + 1082\text{H} = 25A82\text{H} \]
  1. Find the effective address (\(EA\)) and physical address for MOV AX, [BX+SI+0100H] given \(\text{DS} = 3000\text{H}\), \(\text{BX} = 0200\text{H}\), \(\text{SI} = 0050\text{H}\). Solution:
\[ EA = 0200\text{H} + 0050\text{H} + 0100\text{H} = 0350\text{H} \] \[ \text{Physical Address} = 30000\text{H} + 0350\text{H} = 30350\text{H} \]

docs.title: Section 4: Assembly Code & Algorithm Synthesis
docs.text:
1. Write an 8086 assembly program sequence to add two 32-bit numbers stored in memory. Solution: 
    MOV AX, WORD PTR [NUM1_LOW]     ; Load low word of Number 1
ADD AX, WORD PTR [NUM2_LOW]     ; Add low word of Number 2
MOV WORD PTR [SUM_LOW], AX      ; Store low word sum

MOV AX, WORD PTR [NUM1_HIGH]    ; Load high word of Number 1
ADC AX, WORD PTR [NUM2_HIGH]    ; Add high word of Number 2 with Carry
MOV WORD PTR [SUM_HIGH], AX     ; Store high word sum

docs.title: 8. Exam-Oriented Worked Numerical Examples & Step-by-Step Traces
Problem 1: 8086 Physical Address Generation
docs.text:
Question: Calculate the 20-bit Physical Address generated by the 8086 CPU for the following segment and offset register pairs: 1. $ ext{CS} = 2500 ext{H}, ext{IP} = 1200 ext{H}$ 2. $ ext{DS} = 4000 ext{H}, ext{BX} = 0050 ext{H}, ext{SI} = 0100 ext{H}$ (Based-Indexed Addressing) 3. $ ext{SS} = 7000 ext{H}, ext{SP} = 0FF0 ext{H}$

Step-by-Step Solution & Calculation: 1. Case 1 (Code Segment Fetch): - Formula: $ ext{Physical Address} = ( ext{CS} imes 16_{10}) + ext{IP} = ( ext{CS} \ll 4) + ext{IP}$ - $ ext{CS} imes 10 ext{H} = 25000 ext{H}$ - Add Offset $ ext{IP} = 01200 ext{H}$ - $ ext{Physical Address} = 25000 ext{H} + 01200 ext{H} = \mathbf{26200 ext{H}}$

  1. Case 2 (Data Segment Based-Indexed Fetch):
  2. Formula: $ ext{Effective Address (EA)} = ext{BX} + ext{SI} = 0050 ext{H} + 0100 ext{H} = 0150 ext{H}$

  3. $ ext{Physical Address} = ( ext{DS} imes 10 ext{H}) + ext{EA} = 40000 ext{H} + 0150 ext{H} = \mathbf{41500 ext{H}}$

  4. Case 3 (Stack Segment Operation):

  5. Formula: $ ext{Physical Address} = ( ext{SS} imes 10 ext{H}) + ext{SP}$
  6. $ ext{SS} imes 10 ext{H} = 70000 ext{H}$
  7. Add Offset $ ext{SP} = 00FF0 ext{H}$
  8. $ ext{Physical Address} = 70000 ext{H} + 00FF0 ext{H} = \mathbf{70FF0 ext{H}}$
